div.p: 7LADIES' LETTER. MY DEAR NTELLT-R,

As each springtime comes round everybody seems of the opinion that the hats of the season are the prettiest ever seen. Freshness this year is part of their charm. The folds of chiffon or Esse are disposed with a deftness that is invari- ably described by the gazers in bonnet-shop win- dows as "so very French:" Silk, whether plain or tucked or stitched, is as much used for trimmings as the more aerial materials. It has weather- resisting qualities that appeal to the prudent in our changeable climate. A very pretty toque I saw yesterday is made of beige tucked glace silk, arranged in bows and loops above the hair, a couple of ostrich feathers being the only additional trimm- ing. Black chip of the fine and supple sort is as much in favour as ever, holding its own against the endless varieties of coloured straw, much of which more nearly resembles horse-hair in texture, so light and pliable is it.
t 4

I have noticed that chief among the new robe dresses prepared for summer wear are zephyrs in holland colour, trimmed with bands of openwork embroidery. Others are dark blue, pale grey-blue, grey, green, pink, and citron colour, with trim- mings of the Madeira-work or lace, white or ecru. Very smart appeared to be two walking gowns which I saw the other afternoon. One is in pastel. blue faced cloth, with revers of panne. Very narrow tucks are disposed upon skirt and bodice, and form a border round the former. The blue silk Test has bands of the stitched cloth, simulating a pointed yoke. The belt is folded black velvet. ale second one was a tea-coloured voile, made up in perpendicular pleats from a plain piece on the hips, outlined with closely-set rows of machine- stitching. The little bolero was pleated and edged with rows of stitching. The vest was white silk, with rows of stitching in the tan cloth strapped across it. The collar and epaulettes were in guipure, and the tie was in pale blue glace silk.

Boon it s hoped there will be a vogue for parasol covers of cut linen, though this kind of work will perhaps appeal more readily to the housewife for coverlets and tablecloths. Collars made of it, however, would be most smart, and especially for washing linen summer gowns and children's pelisses. I saw a child very nicely dressed the other after- noon. She was wearing a black hat, trimmed in front, which was turned upwards, with velvet and a beautiful black feather. The coat was of a square character with large revers and a collar both edged with velvet.

Reversible wooilens are being employed for the costume tailleur, such as beige one side and orange the other, blue one side and mauve on the reverse, black and white check with cerise on the other side, and so on. These woollens are made with a thick web, and no lining is required, so that the contrast- ing colour on the underneath side shows to advan- tage for revers and trimmings. Mohair repps are also used for spring promenade toilettes, and there is a new bright linen, simulating silk, which will make up well for race gowns and seaside frocks. Lace bolero forms part of some of the new bodices. It does not hang over them' loose and independent, but is fastened down firmly and neatly. The yoke is as much as ever a feature of the newest bodices, and the revers are replaced by a round, flat collar, which shows the shoulder-line to advantage. Sometimes the yolce is a trellis- work of velvet. or narrow white and black ribbon. There is sonic sign of the reappearance of the box- pleat up the front of the new bodices. It is orna- mental, le,,d;ft, tself igieeahly to trimming and buttons. . .
Your loving
JENIsTIL

"Different, say you! I cton't see it; I don't see that usin' that brass o' Steve's is any diff'rent to usin' this brass of Mestur Ralph's, an' there's no diffrence between two, nobbut one were in papper notes an t'others yellow, shiny gowd. If you're not to be bought with th' brass o' th' one you shouldn't be bought with th' brass o' t'other. "Besides," ,continued the loquacious widow, "there's another way of lookin' at it. If you're not goin' to be bought as you say, by usin' this brass we're goin' to be sowd sowd up. Th' land- lord's threatened to put. th' baffles in if we don't pay all th' rent up. We're six weeks owin', an' if it's not paid an' we're not to be bought,' we'll be sowd up, an' turned out into th' street. "An' if that doesn't suit," continued Mrs. Rayburn, "you'll have to sell or pawn your ball- dress, that hoppery cloak, thoose gowd bangles, an' suchlike; that's what you'll have to do, lass." By shewin,g this alternative, Mrs. Rayburn knew that her position would be strengthened. She knew now dear to her vain daughter were the things she bad enumerated.

"You can do as you like with the money," said Ella; "it shall not be said that Ralph Cartleigh keeps me. I'll go back to the mill first." "Just as you like," said her mother. "I shall keep th' brass an' use it. I've not bin feelin' so well lately, an' I'm goin' to buy mysel' some med'cine, an' luxuries an' things." On the following Monday morning Ella's old workmates were surprised to see her at her looms

-All kinds of rumours concerning her had been floating about during the past four weeks. Some of the gossips said she was going out to her lover in South Africa, but when it was known that she had been seeking employment in the district this notion was discarded. It was common knowledge that she had been in Master Ralph's company at Christmas, and it was declared that a match had been arranged between them, and Ella would never more be seen at the mill.

But her appearance at her old position this morn- ing disposed of all speculations and suppositions. Here she was, and here it appeared she was likely to remain for a time. Ella looked somewhat shamefaced and discon- certed when she joined her companions at breakfast- time.
"We thought you'd left us for ever," said one of the aids.
"We heard you were going to be married," said another.
"And going abroad," added a third. To all these and similar remarks Ella had but little to say, and she gave no explanation of the reasons which had caused her to leave the mill for a time.
Before the breakfast half-hour was ended Ben Potter came along and joined the group of girls, a 3 was his wont. From snatches of the conversa- tion he soon discerned the theme under discussion.

"Ella knows when she's well off," he observed, sagely. "She's quite at home here among good friends, an' if she'll take my advice she'll stop here an' not think of goin' away to forrin' parts, or gettin' wed, or doin' any other such outlandish foolishness. There's not much gowd in Lanky- sheer, but there's plenty of cotton, and where's cotton there's p'raps not much gowd but there's middlin' o' silver—a two-three threepenny bits for th' parsons on Sunday—an 'plenty o' copper. "If I were a lass—an' I'm sorry I weren't born one, they're so bonny—if I were a lass, I say, I'd stop in England here for ever an' ever, an' I'd be a owd maid or else wed a chap 'at lives in th' country, a chap 'at had plenty o' brass, smnmat else besides threepenny bits an' copper. But I wouldn't go abroad to outlandish places, no, not for th' best outlandish Outlander under th' sun, not even if he'd crown my yed (head) wi' gowd." "It's a pity you weren't born a lass, Ben," said one of his auditors ; "you'd have made a grand owd woman."

"He's not a bad 'un, now," said another girl. "Hear you, now, that's th' treatment a chap gets after he's bin' givin' away chunks of solid advice. Aye, well, wiunnin will be wimmin, an' lasses will be lasses, an' lads an' lasses will make history an' romance spite of all an owd man can say," and as the warning whistle sounded Ben went off to the warehouse and the girls returned to their looms.

Ella did not take kindly to the weavinm again. Wearying, monotonous toil it appeared to tbe, after the weeks of idleness she had experienced. But the thought that this was the only alternative to dependence on Ralph Cartleigh's charity, spurred her to her task. Yet she had her vacillating moments.

"Perhaps he gave the money without thought of buying his way into favour again," she reflected. "I don't see that I need compromise myself if I do use a little of the money." Then a teasing doubt affected her, and finally she resolved that she would labour on in the mill and thus have the satisfaction of knowing that she was wholly self-dependent. The March day drew to its close.. The sun, dipping in the west, sent a yellow shaft of brilliant light through the weaving- shed, gilding the looms and lightening up the faces of the weavers.
Ella looked yearningly out of the window, then at the clock. .

"Five o'clock!" Ah, how she longed for half- past! Surely this protracted clay would never come to an end! 'Twas the longest and the weariest she had ever experienced at the mill. ' Half-an-hour yet ore sho would be released! Her head ached with the incessant din and rattle of fnachinery ; she was not yet accustomed to the noisy rattle and clatter. As she bent for a moment over the flawless calico, streaming from the loom, a trembling hand clutched her arm and a white, scared face looked into hers.
"You're wanted at home, at once," cried the girl at her side.

"What is it ? " Ella asked in alarm, observing the other's agitation. "Your mother!" gasped the girl, and hurried away. Seizing her hat and shawl, Ella rushed from the mill. Through the 'quiet streets she ran, with agonising thoughts stabbing her at every step. Breathless she reached her home, and, dashing into the kitchen, saw with horror .a doctor and a group of neighbours bent over the prostrate form of her mother, who was lying white and motionless on the sofa.

"She's here," cried the women in chorus as Ella entered; then they quietly left the room. "0 mother Mother What's to do with you ? " cried the anguished girl, as she threw herself down at the couch-side and looked into the deathly face. ".1 don't know, lass; I don't know!" the poor soul cried, feebly. "I'm done for! I'm done for!"
"Oh, doctor, can't you save her? Can't you save her?" sobbed the frenzied girl in wild appeal. The medical man tenderly sought to soothe her and led her aside as he said:

"I have done all I can, my child. The rest must be left to a Higher Physician." "Come here, lass! Come here, Ella!" The dying woman spoke in a low whisper. She was falling fast. "Oh, mother, speak to me; speak to me ! " Ella cried, as she knelt before her parent. "Speak to you; yes, lass! What can I say? God—bless—you! God—bless you! God take care of thee What can I say ? Aye, God take care of thee. Man—will—not—l'm afraid! God— bless—thee!"

A trembling of the lips, a flutter of the eyelids, a spontaneous tremor of the tortured body, and life had departed from it. "Eh, I allus thought •hoo'd go off sudden, poor body," said one of the neighbour women, re-entering the chamber of death. "Heart disease, th' doctor says. Aye, well, it allus tak's 'em sudden. Poor body! Heart disease! Aye, an' her poor lass 'll have a broken heart now. Dear! Dear 1"

div.head: CHAPTER XVIII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVIII.

111 my weeks had passed since the painfully .ivu,:ien death of. Mrs. Rayburn. April's shine and shower was making field and 'zdgerow alive with fair green beauty. The swelling dads on the trees, the sturdy, shining blades of grass, all testified to the glorious revivifying powers of spring. Spring, full of promise and hope; spring, with its healthful breezes, its rejuvenating, life-giving sun, its tears Of sunny joy; spring, the birth-time, when the human heart and spirit leap with external nature into new life and hope. The hum and b-r-r-r of the factories was still heard in Dalesworth ; the clouds of smoke still hung affectionately over the town as if loth to leave it. Morning, noon and night the operatives clattered to and from their work, but Ella Rayburn was not of their number. Dalesworth knew her

div.head: no more,
div.p: no more,
A week after her mother's demise she left the town and went to reside at Southport with her maternal aunt.
Here, amidst new surroundings, she tried to forget the, tragic event which had cast such a deep shadow on her young life. Away from her old home with its sad aweiations, she felt less melancholy.

The salubrious air ot th 3 watering resort, and the quiet, placid life of the town contrasted sharply with the vitiated, thick atmosphere of Dalesworth, and the-constant noise and bustle of machinery. For a time the change of life and scene interested Ella. and distracted her attention, then. she tired of the quietness snd tranquillity of South- port Erna became restless and discontented. • She had written to Stephen Hart, apprising him of her trouble, but many weeks must elapse ere she would receive a letter in reply. During her bereavement Ralph Cartleigh had been most kind and solicitous. He had attended the funeral, and afterwards remained with her in the Quiet house seeking to solace and comfort her. Since Ella had come to Southport, he had written to her, asking forgiveness for his brutal conduct on Boxing Night, in extenuation referring to his inebriated state, when, as he said, "he was not quite responsible for his conduct." Remembering his many kindnesses of late, Ella replied and made light of the incident, giving him. to understand that he occupied the same place .0 here esteem as heretofore. _
At Easter she was visited by the irrepressi* Ralph, who had engaged rooms for the week-eiai at the S- Hotel.

"I've come to cheer you up," he said, in explanation of his visit. "You are in need I cheerful company. Ah, I see Southport is putting roses into your cheeks That's better!" Ella was inclined to protest against this intrusion on her privacy, but .he successfully overcame her objections. "It is not good for man to be alone, nor woman either," he said, gaily. "Especially in Southport, for, though it is a charming town, it loses much of its charm if one lives a lonely life in the place." This Ella had realised. So she fell in with his wishes, and together they passed the time in promenading along Lord-street, the Parade, the straggling pier, from whence they could see across the water breezy Blackpool, where they had speat such a joyous time several months before. • "Do you ever think of our trip to Blackpool? Cartleigh asked, as they stood at the pier-head looking at the Tower in the distance. "Sometimes," she answered, musingly. "And do you think of it with pleasure ? " "Yes, oh, yes," was the impulsive reply. Then as a shadow flitted across her animated face, "Tinged with a little pain," he added. "Ah 1 I forgot I Your mother was with us then." The subject was instantly dropped. Theimlidays being over, Ralph Cartleigh prepared to leave for Dalesworth.
"You are not coining back to us, again, X suppose ? " he observed, as Ella walked with him tl. the railway station. "I think not," she replied. "I don't know. I'm unsettled here."
He looked at her searchingly, and would fain have asked a question, but felt that the time was not yet.

"While you are here may I come to see you occasionally ? " She could not give him a negative reply. He had been very kind to her. She would not compromise herself this time. There was nothing to fear—now. She was convinced that Steve would ask her to join him soon; until then she would act kir dig to this man.
"You may come if you wish, Mr. Cartleigh,* she answered.
Ralph Cartleigh returned to Dalesworth highly elated.

"I am scoring all along the line," he said. "If I only mind my p's and q's I shall win back her confidence again, and once I do that I'll make sure of her once and for all. For two years I have been shuffling about with her, but if all goes well I'll not play the game wore than two months longer, before I make her mine, or as much mine as I desire her to be."

He had no intention of marrying her, not at all. That was as far from his thought as anything possibly could be. She should be his plaything, amuse and minister unto him as he listed, then when he was tired of her he would cast her aside as he had cast others. Such was his thought; Sail: his plan. 'There was still considerable friction between his father and himself; but that was inevitable, the young fellow concluded. When he returned from his holidays his father was, as usual, in a combative humour. "You'll make the North of England intolerable for us to live in soon, young man," were his first words to his recreant son.

"Indeed! In what way ? 7 asked Ralph, in surprise. "In what way! How can you ask?" replied his irate parent. 'ln every way, I tell you. You disgrace your family here in Dalesworth, you dis- grace us at Oldham by masquerading with a hussy whom you took to Blackpool some months before. Now we are informed that you have been seen walking the streets of Southport with this—er— person. ' "I think this person' to whom you so slight- ingly refer is quite as respectable as the tale-bearing informers of whom you appear to think so much," said Ralph. He was nettled at this smug sneer at Ella Rayburn. "She is a low, common, vulgar person," said games Cartleigh, with emphasis. "She would not be in your company if she were not." "Thanks, very much; you are very compli- mentary. Let me see. You are my father, why speak thus? " "Yes, more's the shame and pity." . "I agree with you. More's the shame and pity that I should be related to such a parent. But we'll leave our unsavoury selves, father; neither of us are angels, but the girl you so meanly attack is, at any rate, above reproach." "You are no judge," said his father, con- temptuously. "I wouldn't take your word; it is worthless.'

"Thanks, again," said Ralph, with biting sarcasm. "You consider yourself a good judge, eh? Well, since we'll admit that, I would remind you that you consider the girl whom you malign so bitterly as quite good enough to work in your factory." "She is all right in her place," said the factory.. master.

"In her place!" sneered his son. "Yes, as one of your hands.' As a factory hand she's all right; as a woman possessing a heart or a soul, she's all wrong." "Tush ! Bosh! Rubbish! " exclaimed James Cartleigh. "It is useless talking with such as you." "I've long since come to that opinion concern- ing yourself," rejoined Ralph, "but you will insist on boring me with your talk." "Yon had better clear out of this district altogether," said James Cartleigh, after an eloquent pause. "I don't wish to have more scandal aboit here, and if you persist in parading about pui,lx watering resorts with mill girls, I know how it will end."
"What will you give me to clear out ? " Dowry asked the son, as if engaged in a business transaction.

This blunt query, coming with such suddenness, rather staggered the factory-master. For a moment he did not reply. When he had somewhat recovered from the shock, he looked up at the ceiling and appeared to be engaged in an elaborate calculatica. "How much ? " His son's voice roused him. "I'll give you nothing." "Nothing ! " repeated the young man, echoing the very tone of his parent. "No, not one farthing. You have bled me for years. I have paid your debts—betting debts, too. I've allowed you to rob me do you hear to rob me at all ends. I've done all this, and I'll do it no more. You'll not get a penny from me now, nor will you while I live." "And after you depart, die, go hence, I don't expect much from you." "Not one penny-piece shall I leave you. You've been the curse of my life." _ _ _
"Indeed! ll'm !" ejaculated the flippant young man. "You wouldn't pay my passage, I suppose, out to Tiinbuctoo, say, or the Cannibal Islands? " "Your mother might; I wouldn't."

"Thanks. I have much to thank you for, father —very rn!..,wh," said the scapegrace son in mow serious tone. "Perhaps I've not been all thø model son should have been, but possibly you haven't been a model father, eh ? Like father, 14' son, you know." James Cartleigh did not reply to this piercing thrust. The still small voice of conscience not yet quite dead within him, told him that there wat perhaps much truth in his son's hard words. Maybe he had not done his duty aright, mayhap in the years of the past in his all-loving zeal for money-making, he had neglected to train up this soul—once young—aright, and in so neglecting the sacred trust his own nature had suffered. Bitter, galling, distracting thought! As the stormy interview closed, and the unhappy parent left the room, his son Henry entered. He looked pale and wan, and was evidently far from well. Nevertheless, his manner was as cheery and bright as ever. He advanced to his brother and shook hands with him cordially. "I am pleased to see you, Ralph," he said. Ralph was tempted to make a. sneering reply,

but the bitter wores MICK in ins iiiroat. JIG looked up abashed into the kindly grey eyes of 1315 brother, and felt ashamed as he recollected how wantonly he had squandered the money Henry 124 d lent him. "Oh, that money," he began, as if thinking, ito would be uppermost in the other's mind. "ill', pay you back in a week or two." "Oh, don't trouble," said Henry, "I've neve!: thought of it since. Don't trouble about paying ' back I shan't need it. I'm giving up the vrerk in Ancoats. It was a glorious work, but I'Ve to give it up. My health has been very bad; shall have to go abroad for a time. I'm going out to South Africa." sual "Indeed I" remarked Ralph, manifesting unu interest. _ .

"Yes. I'm called out to the South African mission field, and I've promised to ,c;o. Father knows about it, and mother and Marie; they are sorry, but it is God's will." Ralph Cartleigh regarded his brother keenly an he spoke with great fervour, and evident sincerity, Could he really be sincere? Was he a truly good man, or was he like the rest, ten parts hypocrite tO. one part saint? Clever delineator of huraan character though he was, Ralph could not ;wen" ately probe the depths of his brother's nature. "Henry knocks the heredity theory into th: proverbial cocked hat, if he is a genuine saint, mused Ralph, "for I can't tell from whom he inherits such saintly qualities. All our lot seep to have a leaning to the other undesirable set. Nnt he's no saint," he concluded. "He's as muck!' sinner and a humbug as dad or myself, only ne conceals the fact more skilfully." Henry spoke enthusiastically of the work before, him. The natives were in need of Christian teach- ing ; they were hungering for the Gospel, which would emancipate them soul and body. "Don't you think you'd better go and Christiania° the Boers?" said Ralph. "They appear to be 9.5 much in need of Christianity as the niggers." f "There are good Christians amonLst them, J• understand."

"Psalm-singing humbugs, I reckon. If they are Christians; why don't they treat our countrynie° in a Christian fashion.? Why do they continue to oppress the Outlanders ? " "I am not a politician, brother. I am a minister of the Gospel," Henry replied, evasively. (c Most of these Outlanders go to seek for gold; I go to seek for souls—precious souls, lost in heather' darkness." _ _

"Well, I wish you a good harvest, brother. rot my part I should go on the gold lay. Nigger souls won't amount to much when you've saved 9 hundred of them. An ounce of gold would be worth more than the whole lot."
Henry Cartleigh smiled sadly. He was not to be drawn into controversy by his cynical brother. His duty was clear. No scorn, no ridicule should cause him to neglect it. (To be continued.)

div.p: "WOMEN'S CHAT."

"Of all the events of a man's life," said Selden, "his marriage does least concern other people, yet of all actions of our lives 'tis most meddled with by other people." This remark is especially applicable to the marriage of Royal personages, as we knew from many examples. Busy-bodies among writers for the press, have married tne young Queen of Holland to half the bachelor Princes of Europe, and they have also caused a good deal of annoyance to the Austrian Imperial Family, by annortnciag the engagement of the Archduke Franz Ferdinand, to the Countess Sophie Chotck. Tbe most minute particulars have been printed with regard to this supposed approaching marriage, and some of those writers who know the business of Royal Families, better than the Families themselves, have announced the title which the Emperor had conferred upon the Countess. The nuisance at length became so intolerable that an emphatic official centradiction was published, but that does not disconcert the gossips, who still declare that the Archduke looks unhappy, and not satisfied with his present life. Perhaps the explanation Is that he wants to emigrate to some island where the people mind their own business. Mr. W. H. Wilkins. M.A. has been at great pains to ascertain accurately,the history of Sophie Dorothea, who at the age of 16, was married to the Hanoverian Prince, who became afterwards Geoige I. of England. The story follows from beginning to end, the lines of the most approved Adelphi drama. There is the young wife wronged and neelested, owing mainly to the machina- tions of a designing woman, the arrival upon the scene of the villain of the piece a Count, rich and handsome, a Projected elopement, defeated by the secret murder of the Count ; and the condemnation of the Princess to life- long imposontnent in a Castle. It will be claimed by some people that Mr. Wilkins'bo_k clevates"the legitim- ate drama" to a new plane. Prince-s Cbrittien, among her multitudinous other duties still finds time to take an interest in the poultry industry. She is the head of the Executive Committee of the National Poultry Organisation Society.which was formed About two years ago, to promote the develop- ment of poultry breeding. The society distributes leaf- lets, providing information upon the various aspects of , poultry keeping, and it assists in establishing depots, where produce can be collected at local centres, ants marketed to the best advantage. The society has only been able, so far, to carry op, operations upon a small scale, but these have already resulted in consideraWe financial benefit to the farmers and cottagers in the dis- tricts where it has been possible to establish local depots. What is now desired, is that some one in the country districts, should tame the initiative in forming a branch, and the society will gladly reader any asaistanes in its power upoe application to the secretary at the cfices 12, Hanover-square London, W. Among many Influential persons, associated with the Society, are Lord Rothschild, the Duke of Rutland. Lord Wantage, Sir John Lewes, Lord Windsor' and Sir James Blyth. There are also on the Ex cutiveCommittee be- slues Princess ( hristian, the Countess of Arran:Via- eounteas Cranbome, the Hon. Sybil Amherst, the ROD; Florence Amherst, and Miss Smith Dentin. Though much may be done by well directed effort to benefit the home production of poultry, and eggs, the returns show that we import more of this produce from abroad than ever. Australia is even sending us eggs, and large quantities are imported from the Continent, packed in cases, or drums, without the shells. They are used in hotele,and by large confectioners, and others requiring large quantities of (ggs. The returns show that we are now payiag about £6.000,000 a year for foreign eggs, and people often wonder why these could net be produced, and at least a large part of the money earned at home. It is, however, not the case as is usually announced, that this country is as suited as any other to poultry keeping. As all poultry farmers are aware, the one thing above all others whicti checks egg production is a damp soil, especially in a cold climate, and in both, these respects, such countries as France or Italy offer great advantages to the poultry keeper. Much has been said from time to time about the deadly weapons with which we ~secure our headgear to la our heads, ud no doubt there ailh grounds for the many scathing comments directed against teo in the use of the modern hat pin. That it is a source of considerable danger is unquestionable. But we are going to alter all that. Not by returning to our old, and inartistic friend —the e astic band, but by means of an improved pin, which, while it safely secures the headgear to the head is so manipulated as to be perfectly harmless to our- selves, and our near neighbours. The invention will shortly be on the market, and seems likely to prove a teem and a blessing to womenkind in general—and men- kind to, with their wholesome timer of the up-to-date dagger. Gold and silver chain purses are in great favour, hung either from the waist, or the wrist. Undoubtedly. the latter mode of wearing them is the sater,especially those manulactured of the more costly metal. Suspended from a strong flexible chain,they occupy a comparatively sate position, and when additional security is desirable, can easily be grasped in the hand. A life s'ze statue of solid gold tisq this advantage, it can always be melted down and turned to practical us,. The Americans long ago announced the intention of etend• ing a gold statue to the Paris exhibition, and though a little late it is still proposed to carry out the idea. The figure, which is being made by Miss Bersy Potter for the exhibit of the State of C•loradn, stands sft. sin. in • height, and has for its model, Miss Maude Adams, one of the favourites of the American stage. It conta.:ns nearly 7 cwt- of pure sold the value of the metal being not far short of £50,000. This is the first golden statue of which there is any record, in modern times, but there was one of solid silver—that of Miss Ada Rehan—at the World's Fair at Chicago, seven years ago. Society has discovered a new variation of the " book" and "flower" parties which have lately been the fashion. It seems to say much for lack of occupation or brains, that people should always be searching into the realms of puzzledom for freeh means for killing time, but so it is. Instead et wearing a decoration representing the name of a book or flower which the others had to guess— each ,ne brings a photograph of himself or herself taken 1 when he, or she, was more or less small. The photo- graphs are then handed round to the assembled guests, who endeavour to name the originate, a prizs being given to the one who identifies the greatest number:

div.head: CHAPTER XVII.
div.p: CHAPTER XVII.

After Boxing Night's distressing experience Ella Rayburn decided to leave Fernleigh Mill at the year-end and seek work elsewhere. She had no desire to meet Ralph Cartleigh again. The vicious, brutal side of his nature, which the girl first saw on the terrible night of the ball, appalled her, and she shrank from the thought of again being pestered by him. The gold necklet, the bangles, and other pretty presents she had received from him were very precious to her, and she had no desire to part with them. His presents were good if he was bad. She told her mother of her intention to leave the mill.

"You musn't think of doin' any such thing," said Mrs. Rayburn. "Leave th' mill, indeed! An' where are you likely to find another shop? Not at any other mill in Dalesworth, I know. They're stoppin' a lot of their reg'lar hands as it is, an' it isn't likely they'll take you on in that case." "I think I can get in at Dobson's," said Ella. _ _ _ _ _

"You think; yes, but you're not sure. Stay where you are an' be content. An' what are you wantin' to leave for? Just because Mestur Ralph were a bit silly on th' ball night. Bless you, when a chap's got a sup of drink in him he doesn't know what he's doin'. He meant no harm, not him, indeed Think nowt no more about it, an' go back to your work as usual." But Ella was determined to leave, and leave she did at the week-end.

As her mother had predicted, however, work was not easy to obtain, and her search for a position at the neighbouring mills was unavailing. It was disheartening work on these cold January days to go from place to place and ever receive the same negative.,reply. "You'll have to go beak to th' owd place," said Mrs. Rayburn one evening as Ella returned after her usual fruitless search.

"Never I'll go and beg my bread before I'll go back there again," was the spirited reply. "Well, we shall see. • We shall have to start beggin' pretty soon, too, for we've done about all th' borrowin"at we can. We've no brass to go buy stuff at th' Store, an' I've run up as big a score at Sefton's as he'll let me. lie wants some brass, he says, before he trusts us with any more." Ella bit her lips in vexation; it was very annoy- ing to be in such a plight, in mid-winter, too. All the money Steve had sent had long been spent; the last shilling went in the purchase of the opera cloak. Of her earnings at the mill little had been saved. "They made straight wi' th' brass as it came," as the local folks said, living from hand to mouth. "We shall•have to manage somehow," said Ella. "I shall get in somewhere soon, perhaps." "Oh, aye," remarked her mother. "We'll get in somewhere else sooner though I'm thinkin', an' that's the workhouse. Couldn't you let Steve know how we're fixed ? "

"No," said Ella, finally, and her tone indicated that her mind was at any rate made up on that point. Bitter though their poverty was, the widow and her proud daughter endeavoured for a time to dis- guise the ugly, painful fact. Each week-end Ella arrayed herself in her finery, and the widow donned her showy silk dolman. But as February, with its bleak, searching winds, and sloppy days, set in, and the larder had become totally denuded of food, Mrs. Rayburn, unknown to her daughter, went to Fernleigh Mill and had an interview with the manager, Ralph Cartleigh. The young man had not seen Ella since the night of the ball, and had wondered at her absence from the mill, but hearing the gossip that was flying about amongst the operatives, he soon ascertained the cause.

"She's made too much fuss about the affair," said he to himself. "I'll see her and soon make things right, when I get other matters settled." "Other matters " were chiefly of a domestic character. r James Cartleigh had heard from many friends and acquaintances that his son was masquerading at the Ball with on of his weavers, the pair of them being highly inebriated when they left the hall. Father and son had a battle-royal over this affair. Up to the time of Widow Rayburn's visit to him, Ralph Cartleigh had not succeeded in pacifying his irate parent. James Cartleigh was highly indignant at his son's indiscreet behaviour, and would listen to no defence or explanation which crafty Ralph endeavoured to offer. Mrs. Rayburn was ushered into the manager's private office, and the doors being closed, soon made her business known. "Our Ella's not a bad sort, but she's a bit touchy, ' " said the widow, in final explanation of her daughter's attitude. "I understand," said Master Ralph. "She is, as you say, a trifle 'touchy'; perhaps too much so. Kindly tell her from me that I apologise for—er— what shall I say ?—for my indiscreetness." "Oh, it's all right," said the widow, desirous of helping him out. "Yes, you and I understand, Mrs. Rayburn. Christmas festivities—took a drop too much—got over the line, and—er—forgot myself. You know!" "Yes, I know. It's all right. Think nowt about it, Mestur Ralph; I don't. It's nowt but what lots o' young chaps does when they're a bit foolish (beg pardon, I didn't mean exactly that). Think nowt about it. Our Ella will not, I'll warrant, when she's got work again. She's a bit bothered now, an' little things like that upset her a lot." "Tell her that she can start work here any day that she cares to come," said Cartleigh. "Thank you, I will, 3lestur Ralph," the widow replied, as she moved towards the door. "And—here, Mrs. Rayburn!" He took out his purse and gave her a couple of sovereigns. "You don't need to say anything." . . _ _
-"Thank you; Oh, thank you, ever so much," said the delighted woman. never expected, I never-' _ _

He conducted her to the door,and curtseying and murmuring her thanks sheleft him. Ella Rayburn was resolute in her determination not to return to Fernleigh Mill. Ralph Cartleigh's apologies, .as expressed through her mother, she received without one word of comment. For several days Mrs. Rayburn stocked the table with many little delicacies, and Ella wondered where the money came from to purchase them. She was soon enlightened. Returning home early one afternoon, she saw on the kitchen table several gold coins.
"Whose are these ? " she asked, in surprise. "Whose should they be but ours?" returned her mother.
"Who has sent _them ? "

"Who do you think ? " "I cannot tell. I'm no good at guessing," Ella answered, impatiently. "Well, look well at 'em, an' see if they're good un's, an' see if they're made in Afriky or England." They were English coins, sovereigns and half- sovereigns. "Now, you couldn't guess who has sent all that gowd ; no, not if you tried for a month, I reckon?" "No, I don't think I Could," said Ella, more impatiently. "Tell me." "Well," said Mrs. Rayburn, with marked emphasis, "th' chap 'at has brought all that brass an' given it us is th' best friend you or I have, although you think, p'raps, he's your worst enemy." "Ralph Cartleigh ? " gasped the girl. "Yes, Ralph Cartleigh it is, an' I tell you he's not as black as he's painted. I've told you that before, but just because he makes a bit of a slip, you set yoursel' again him." "I want none of his money," said the girl, con- temptuously. "No, p'raps not, lass, but I do. I'm not goin' to starve an' pinch mysel', nor see you do either so long as I can get brass given to me by a decent man." _ _

"I'm not going to be bought," cried Ella, indignantly. "No, but you're going to be sold," her parent retaliated. "You're goin' to be taken in with your own particular self if you're not careful. Don't be so touchy an' particular, lass; you'll never get on in th' world if you are, specially with men-folk. What's th' use of talkin' as you do, sayin' as you're not goin' to be bought? Mestur Ralph doesn't want to buy you,. because of this; he's given it to us ; given it of his own free Will, just as Steve Hart gave us twenty pounds two or three months since. You didn't tulk of Steve buyin' you, then. We used th' brass an' were thankful 'for it." "That case was different," said Ella, seeking to justify herself. "Different 1" exclaimed the widow, now roused to anger by fear that the money supply might be cut off by her daughter's imprudence.

THE telegraph annihilates distance, and the met'. eenger boy kills time. "My father is a great believer in bicycling." "Is he a dealer ? " "N 0 ; doctor." A SCHOOLBOY wrote :—" Soldiers are of three kinds—tin soldiers, real soldiers, and Volunteers." TEACHER "What is a pedestrian ? " Johnny Squanch : "A fellow that gets run over by a bicycle, ma'am."

OLD LADY: "He went where the rneasles were, and of course, he caught than." Young Lady: "Rash, wasn't he ? SHE : "Mr. De. Brush is an impressionist, isn't he ?" THE HORSE BLEM FIEST.—" Take this tube," observed the vet, to his new assistant, fill it with this powder, put it in the horse's mouth and then blow hard." " Yes, sir,' replied he, as he went off gaily to his task. Ten minutes after he re-ap- peared bent double, his face exhibiting the MOO horrible contortions. "Goodness ! what is the matter? Did you do as I told you ?" "I did," gasped the new assistant; " I put the tube in the horse's mouth, but the horse blew first."

THE MONEY'S WORM. —Mr. N., a struggling lawyer in a small Scotch town, received a call trom a farmer who wanted legal advice. Mr. N. took down a much-used volume from his small book case, and gave the required advice, for which he charged the modest sum of fifteen shillings. His client handed him a one-pound note. With a troubled look Mr. N. took it. He flushed in the face as he passed his fingers nervously through his pockets, and his embarrassment increased as he continued his search among the papers on his desk. "Well," said he, taking down the law-book again and turning over ther pages, "I'll give you five more shillings' worth of advice." "A MISTAKE.—A merchant, who could neither read nor write, used to keep his own accounts by drawing the shape of each thing he sold, and put- ting the price by the side of it. One day a farmer came to pay for things he had bought. The mer- chant took down a book, and had mentioned several of the things, when he came to a cheese. "That must be wrong," said the farmer, "for I always make my own cheese,and have never bought one." "Oh," said the merchant, "but you must have had it, for I have marks in my book for the shape of a cheese." "Perhaps it was a grind- stone," said the farmer, "I remember buying one about that time." "The very thing," said the merchant, "I forgot to put the hole in the middle, and mistook it for a cheese 1"

div.head: MISTAKE
div.p: MISTAKE

The Chairman said that at the last meeting of the Parhh Council there WA!, some doubt as to "bother the annual perhli meeting should have been held, and the Clerk was instructed to write to the Local Government Board about the matter. The Clerk reed the reply which he had received which was to the effect that although in pursuance of the Parish Councillors Tenure of office Act an election of parish councillors did not take place, it seemed to the ' Board that the annual assionbly of tee perish meeting should tieverthelees have been held as directed by the Local Government Act of 1897. It did not appear to the Board that the recent Act affected the matter. The failuro to hold the annual a,eembly could no: be rem( died and it did not appear to the Board to be necessary that a parish meeting should now be held in substitution of I.le annual as7embly. The Chairman saii it appeared they had evidently committed an error by not holding the meeting between March and April. Although they were heeling it now it did not quite take the place of the meeting they should base need. Mr. Jenkins : I don't think the Council ought to be blamed in the matter. The Council is really not to blame but the clerk (Mr. Woodcock) is abs)luiely. Cori- tiouine, Mr. Jenkins said that after the advice tendered to the Clerk he really thought it was something more than a mistake. Having met a member of the Council lait Wednesday week arid hearing that no reply had Leon received concerning the matter he wrote to the Local Government Board and placed the matter before there. He waited until the following Tuesday morning and not having received a reply he wrote to Mr. T. W. Ru.sseill, the member of Parliament for South Tyrone who was also Parliamentary Secretary for the L ,cal Government Board and on the following Thursday Mr. Wuoacock re- ceived a reply and he (Mr Jenkins) received a similar letter. The Board left it to them to say what should be done for the neeleot of the Clerk lee took it, who was absolutely responsible for what had occurred. The Chairman : There is no gainsaying it. There has been neglect and a meeting ought to have been held. The Clerk said he concluded there would be no neces- sity for a meeting as there was no election of parish councillors. He mentioned three other Councils who had done the same thing including Stockton Heath. Mr. Jenkins : Stockton Heath have to hold their meeting: and there are likely to be serious consequences. Mr. Long said that the Clerk had evidently made a mistake but they were all subject to mistakes and he moved that the business of the meeting be proceeded with. The motion was seconded and carried, Mr. Jenkins being the only disentierit. THE VILLAGE POMP. Mr. Pearson said that most of those present krove there had been some friction concerning the water from the pump in Knot sford-road. Elle believed the Rural District Council, through their inspector having had the water analysed, condemned it as beieg unfit for domes- tic purposes. A further sample of the same water analysed by the same analyst was, however, reported to be an excellent water, in fact of good degree. He was one who used the water and appreciated it. Recently the pump had been cleaned out and some alterations made thereby undergoing expense which be supposed would be borne by the pariih of Grappenhall. He moved "That immediate steps be taken to obtain the absolute control by the Parish Council of the pump in Knutsford- road." Mr. Jenkins said be could quite understand the Rural District Council interfering to take a sample of the water but be could not understend why the Rural Council should take the pump up and alter the position of it. As Mr. Pearson said, he bad no doubt that the parish directly or indirectly would have to meet the ex- pense. Were not they as a parish entitled to do what might be neaessary to the pump independent of submit- ting to the analysis ? He seconded Mr. Pearson'e resolu- tion. 'Jibe Chairman : Who does the pump belong to ? Mr. Jenkins . The parish. It is a public pump. Mr. Jenkins read the act relating to the powers vested by Parish Councils which stated " amongst other powers which they possess is the one to utiiise any well, spring, or stream within their par:sh and provide facilities for obtaining water therefrom but so as not to interfere with the rights of any Corporation or person." Mr. Long said that be was the original owner of the well and it wee fenced off from the road. It eras, how- ever, an open well and people were in the habit of making use of it. Several times he had feund tramps washing their feet in it and he determined to put a stop to it. He created a pump at his own expense for the, use of himself and his neighbours. Some little time ago he was served with notice by the Rural District Council : that the water had been analysed and found unfit for domestic use. He saw the nuisance inspector and after- wards wrote to the Dist-rict Council saying that now there was a public body taking charge of such wells he was quite willing to band any rights he might have in the matter to the District Council. The water bad been analysed several times and he thought that rather than do away with the pump it would be better to clean it out. He told the Council he would give them any help he could in the work. He thought they would agree with him that after this there was no need for any such ebullition of feeling by passing the resolution. It was in the hands of the District Council to see that,the supply was good. After some discussion the resolution was carried by a majority of five. The Chairman : It will rest with the discretion of the Parish Council afterwards to discuss the matter. TEIE ASSESSMENT OF COTTAGEe. Mr. Pearson askeo if the Clerk would tell him how the Assessment Committee for the parish was formed, and who the members were ? The Clerk : The Assessment Committee is formed from the Rural District Councillors whe form themselves into Committees for various purposes. Mr. Bradford, the representative of the parish on the Rural Connell supplied the names of the members of the Committee. The Clerk stared that a new valuation list was being prepared on the basis of the rent paid with certain deductions allowed by the Committee on different classes of property, such as 20 per cent. on parks and places not inhabited; 12A. per cent.on buildings over £2O ; 15 per cent tram £8 to £2O ; 25 per cent. on cottage property under ; land without build- ings 5 per cent. The new valuation list increased their valuation on the gross to £8240 103 from £BO5B, an increase of £lB2 102. The ratable value was £7,219. Mr Jenkins said that the question was as to who were the assessors for parish property. He understood that the committee althoueh formed for the purpose really did not assess the property but only adjudicated in cases of appeal. He might say that. both he and Mr Pearson, and he daresay Mr Jones, who was also a neighbour felt rather hurt, as they thought there was some little neglect in the assessing of the cottages in which they lived. In 1897 these cottages were assessed at £7 10s Od, when the clerk occupied one of the cot- tages. Directly the clerk left the house the assessment of each of the cottages was raised from £7 10s 0d to £lO. Now it followed that either the cottages were not sufficiently assessed whilst the clerk was residing in one of them, or else they were over assessed since he left. An advance of more than one fifth of the assessment of cottages of that class seemed to him to be a very big jump indeed. He had been assured by the clerk and re- presentative on the Rural Council that the assessment was done by tOe overseers or assistant overseer and that the committee only acted in cases of appeal. The Chairman : The responsibility rests with:the com- mittee and not the subordinates. Mr. Jenkins said that if the clerk thought an assess- ment at £7 104 0.1 was sufficient when residing in one of the cottages, how could he possibly conceive that the value of the cottages had risen so suddenly and so greatly as to allow an increase of more than one filth? The Chairman: I think the suggestions are unworthy of the parish meeting. The matter then dropped, and the meetietconcluded.

div.head: FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNI-
div.p: FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNI-
VEIRSARY.
THE ANNUAL MEETING.

Tile annual meeting was held in the chapel last ni.zht Mr W. Silcock presided and was supported by the Rev Grainger Hargreaves, of China, Major-General Campbral, circuit ministers and others. The Rev. T BISHOP read a letter he had received from Mr Elwin Richardson, of Paddington House, who had been announced to preside, regretting that the state of his health uould prevent him from attending. He enclosed £5 towards the missionary funds. The rev gentleman said he was sure they all sympathind witn Mr Richardson in his sickness, and if the meeting agreed he would write to him expressing their sympathy. (Applause;) Mr. W SILCOCK then took the chair. During the course of his remarks he expressed regret at the abvn of Mr Richardson. He considered it no mean honour to preside at that meeting. They were fortunate in having on the platf‘rm General Campbell who had lived for 40 years in India, and therefore represented a population of 250,000,000 and the Rev. Grainger liar greaves who for many years lived in China, and represented a population of 400,000.000. (Laughter and applause.) It was not necessary for him to sAy anythinS about the cause they were met to advocate. They all knew the need of the Gospel. The Gospel had made this country the highest of nations. Thy koew th need of the Gospel in Asia, that dirk continent full of wicked ness and wrong, and they also knew the need of the- Gospel in Africa and in Europe,including Italy,Germany Russia and France. They saw in their own country the need of the Gospel.

The Rev. H. G. ROBERTS presented the annual report which stated that there was an increase of £l,lOO in the total income of the Wesleyan Foreign Missionary Society for the past year. The amount received, including a balance in hand from the year 1897, account WaP £130,533. MI the expenditure had been mA and £67 carried forward to next year. The net amount contri- buted by the Liverpool District (of which the Warring- ton Society was a part) was £7,119. That circuit had contributed £199 a decrease on the previous year of £l7. The branch in connection with Bold-street Church had contributed £45. The report of the work was most encouraging all round. The various missionary deputa tions rep)rted from all parts of the United Kingdom the growth of the missionary conviction and feeling. The public meetings had been imrroved an I local organisa- tion rendered more efficient. The Rev. GRA.INGER HARGRE&VES delivered a most interesting address on missionary work in China. Be said that the missionaries were not only giving religion to the Chinese, but they were giving them civilisation. and were regenerating society. To-day the Chinese worshipped the past. They could not look forward with hope or pleasure or delight to the future. Their future was dark and unpromising. l'hey worshipped their ancestors and whilst they did so it was impossible to make progress. Whilst they had ancestral worship they had also infanticide. The preaching of the Gospel would bring about a total re- volution in the social life of the Chinese and establish a right relationship between the master and servant and ruler and ruled.

(Applause.) Toe speaker proc, eded to give a most interesting account of his experiences in India. He said he had seen many soldiers in Securd9raNd converted and spoke of the beautiful litt'e church which had been erected there. They ought to tak 3 the deepest interest in their soldiers and sailors. They seat out not only their inissionaries but also their soldiers and.sailors to all the parts of the empire and they were their witness( s as regarded the truth of God. It was not tracts that they wanted (although he did not undervalue them) but the living epistles of the Lord Jesus Christ. The usual votes of thanks concluded the meeting which was of a very interesting character.

div.head: SUICIDAL MANIA AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: A SUICIDAL MANIA AT WARRINGTON.
A Dose of Carbolic Acid.

Mr. Brighouse cenducted inquiries at Warrington on Tuesday into the circumstances attending the deaths of three persons who had committed euicida whilst of un- sound minas. The first was that of John Smith, 39 years of age, a wiredrawer, residing at 10, New-street, who died at his residence at 4 p.m. on Thursday last week from the effects of carbolic acid p lisoning. It appears that deceased had been suffering from the ill- effects of rheumatic fever which afflicted him in October last. At 7.30 a.m. on Thursday the deceased got up and went downetairs. Shortly afterwards his wife followed him and found him lying on the sofa, moaning and un- able to swak. Dr. McCarthy was called in and at- tended the deceased until his death, which took place at the time already indicated. The deceased's wile on go- ing into an outhouse found a bottle containing carbolic acid. The decaased's lips and mouth p eseated the ap- pearance of his having taken some acid. Dr. McCarttey stated that the deceased was under hin care in October wLen be was suffering from rheumatic lever. He was called in to sea him on Thursday last week. He did not suspect that the deceased had taken carbolic acid at that time. Deceased died the same afternoon. Assisted by Dr. Bowden, witness made a post mortem examination. There was a mark on the deceased's lips and chin about two inches long. On opening tte body there was a strong smell of carbolic aeid.—The cause of death was carbolic acid poisoning. The deceased's heart was twice as large as tho normal S
A verdict of •'Suicido whilst cf unsound mind " was returned.
An Ironworker Shoots Himself.

An inqeest was subsequently held on the body of Thomas Nolan, 31 years of age, an ironworker, of 15, Fairclough's-avenue, who died from the effects of a pistol shot early last Friday morning. The Ceroner read the police report from which it appeare I that the deceased went to the house of his father-in-law, John Riley, general labourer, of 15,James- street, on 'thursday evening under the influence ef drink. Be had then with him a revolver which he toyed with all the evening and he also produced a number of cartridges stating that be would put a shot into his head. About one o'clock in the morning the deceased went into the yard and immediately afterwards, the report of a pistol shot was heard. Riley hurried out and found deceased lying with his head resting on the ash-tub, apparently dead. Tne matter was reported to the police and on Sergeant Williamson and P.C. Bruen going to the house, tee de- ceased was found to be quite dead with a bidet wound the right temple. A revolver lay at his feet and con- eained eue spent carridge. The deceased had been in ery low spirits for same time. Mr. T. Daintith, gunsmith, of Bridge-street, stated that the eec3ased bought the revolver produced, which was a cheap one, on Thursday evening. He did not buy Any cartridges. He came baek again at about 9 o'clock in a drunken condition. He said that he wanted some certridges. Witness gave him half-a-dozen " blanks." He wanted to see one shot so they discharged one in the workshop. Witness was under the impression that the man picked a ball cartridge up from the counter whilst his (witness's) back was turned. Sergeant Williamson stated that on Friday morning lee was called to the house of deceased's father-in-law. He fouod the deceased had a bullet wound in his right temple. A s.x-cLambered revolver which contained one spent cartrldeo was by his side. _ _
A vadict of "suicide whilst of unsound mind "was returned.

div.head: Porter Hangs Himself. Sad Case.
div.p: A Porter Hangs Himself. Sad Case.

The jury then invired into the circumstances relative to the death of Thomas Savage, who committed suicide by hanging himself at his residence, 6, Williamson's Square, Church-street. The Coroner read the police report which stated that the deceased had lately 13.:en upset about a debt for which judgment had been obtained against him in the County Court. He had told his wife that he would never pay and that he would die first. He went to work the previous morning and returned at three o'clock ia the afternoon. He went out again and returned at six o'cloc.ll after which he remained in the house and seemed in fairly good spirits. At 930 his wife went to bed leaving him in the kitchen witheut a light. The son Joseph went to sleep on the sofa. After being in la-ezi for some time the wife cams downstairs to see why her husband had not come to bed. She found the de- ceased hanging by the neck from the banisters with the rope which be used in his business as a porter. The son went for assistance and a man named Richards came to the house. He left the deceased hanging and went to the Police Station. Sergeant Williamson and P.C. Brun went and cut the man down when life was found to be

Toe deceased's widow stated that deceased had told her that before he would pay the money he would suffer death. The debt amounted to £3 53 and the costs to £l. He bad to pay 3,4 per mouth. The Coroner : If all pope who owed £4 Si took away their lives there would not be many of ua here. William Richard, a pay;or's labourer rusidisag at 9, Williamson-square, said he was juat going to bed when deceased's son came and toll him tat his father was hurt. When he saw the man hanging it took him by surprise and he went straight away to tho Police Station and told Sergeant Williamson. The Coroner: The Sergeant hag not supernatural powers. Why did nlt you cut him down ? Wit.ness : It takes a man with a nerve.
The Coroner : It was a fit of nervousness you had. Wi:ness Yes sir. It was the first time I aaw a thing like that and I was taken unawares.
The Coroner: You are not labouring; under the de- lusion that no person is entitled to cut down a body eX- cept the police. No sir.
Witness :

Sergeant Williamson stated thgt at 10 10he wag called to the house. Lie and P.C. Bruen fouud the deceased hanging by the rope produced from the stair banisters. They at once cut him down and cgrried him into the kitchen. They applied artificial respiration for about 15 minutes but without success. re body was warm but there were us signs of life. Toe jury returned a verdict of " Suicide whilst of un- sound mind."

div.head: FATALITY AT MESSRS. WALKER'S
div.p: FATALITY AT MESSRS. WALKER'S
BREWERY.
Crushed by a Railway Waggon.

At the Police Station, on Wednesday evening, Hr. Brighouse conducted an inquiry respecting the death of a brewery labourer named Stephen Mannion, 67 years of age, who was killed in the yard of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sens, Limited, earlier in the day.—Major Roe. H M Ins iector of Factories watched the proceedings. Mr. W H J Jenkins repreeented the firm and Mr. R Wool, goods agent for the London and North Western Railway was preeent on behalf of the Cempatiy. The Coroner briefly detailed the facts of the case to the jury. That morning George Ryder, in the employ of the London and North Western Railway Company, was following his usual shunting operations in the yarl of Messrs. Peter Walker wed Sons. He was in tho act of taking an empty waggon drawn by two horses to the leading stage, when be saw Maunion about six yards aways from the end of the eta,ge. He gave the signal that he was starting but after he had gone a few yards a workman shouted out that the deceased was between the stage and the waggon. The deceased was blind in the left eye and no doubt did not see the waggon as it parsed hire. He died shortly after being extricated. Mary Weleh stated that the devased was her brother aed he was 67 years of age. She had not seen him since last Walking Day. He had been a widower for the past 19 years. George Ryder stated that he was engaged in shunting operations about 945 that morning. He saw the de- ceased in a man-hole when he gave the signal that he was going to draw the waggon to the stage. He went to the front horse and had reached the stage when ho herd Philip Cork cry out that there was someone be- tween the stage and the waggon. He stopped the waggon and helped to extricate the deceased. D. Nuttall was sent for but the deceased expired within three minutes from being extricated.

By Major Roe : There was a distance of about six inches between the stage and the waggon. By Mr. Jenkins : The shun:ing operations were en- tirely under the control of the Londoa and North-Wes- tern Railway Company. He laad been ten years in the einnloy of the company. He gave what be thought was sufficient warning. By the Coroner: The deceased would have been all right if Le had remained where he was. Mr. Jenkins : He was practically a supe.aanuated man and did odd jobs about the yard. He really did no manual labour.
Mr. David VVellq, en behalf of the firm, corroborated tbi RtAtemect.
The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental Death ." Mr. Jenkins said the firm would do all they could to see that the deceased was decently buried.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH.

STOCKTON HEATH AND WILDERSPOOL JUVENILE BENEFIT SOCIETY —Oa Tuesday at the Et-iter veitrc meeting in conoection witu the St. Thomas's Churcli, the Vicarortm presided, referred to the progress of tha atove society. He said that this was really not part of the business bf the vestry meeting, but a short time ago the matter was mentioned. 0;. ing to the generosity of Mr. Robert Davies the society was in a satisfactory position. The society was founded about 70 years ago, bui; new rules had been recently drawn up and registered. Mr D ivies had saved the society from going to wreck, and now everything was in good workieg order.

div.head: Parish Council Meeting.
div.p: Parish Council Meeting.

A meeting of the Stockton Heath Paribh Council was held on Tuesday evening in the schoolroom. M. Fred Pearson presided, and there were also present Meesrs. J H Clarke, J Whitley, G El Mason, J Fairhurst, W Mclntyre, and E Bradshaw (clerk).

div.head: WARRINGTON AND NORTHWICH LIGHT RAILWAY.
div.p: THE WARRINGTON AND NORTHWICH LIGHT RAILWAY.

Toe Clerk read a letter he had received from the Clerk to the County Council acknowledging the rec-ipt of the resolution passed at the last meeting of this Council and stating that be would bring it before th,3 Parliamentary Committee. At the same time he pointed out th it it was quite open to the Parish Council to raise the q.lesiin as to the width of the roads before toe Ltit Rail way Commissioners when they held their Equiry, and he suggested that the Parish Council should take steps with a view to that bsing done. Mr. Macon: Yo is have heard nothing further? The Clerk.

The Chairman : Nor about the enquiry itself? The Clerk: N. I asked the Towo Gerk the other day had there been any application for the Town Hall and he said not. Mr. Mason : What notice will tiny giv4 ? The Chairman said there would be a notice in the local papers. The Clerk: I should think they will give 14 days' notice.
Dar. Whitley : It appears from that latter that the Parish COLUIGIi will hava a locus stancli at the enquiry.
ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN

The Chairman said the next business was the election of a chairman for the ensuing year. He had much pleasure in proposing the elec'ion of Mr MA9OI. With the exception of himself, Mr Mason was the oldest mem- ber present and he had alsa brought an intelligent view to bear u-,ou the business of the Council. He had always been vfiy attentive and possessed every quadfication La the position. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Clarke seconded, and said that Mr :Ass m, from his numerous attendances at the meetings of the Coun- cil, possessed a full knowled2e of the buiiness of the township, and he had the ability to coodu.lt the busi- ness in the manner in which it ought to tie. Mr. Whitley supported the motion which was passed. Mr. Pearson said that in giving up the office of chair- man, after having occupied it for three years he must express his thanks to the members for the assistance they ha l given him and the courtesy with which they had always treated him. Hz hoped they would treat his successor with equal kindness. Mr. Whitlcy proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Pearson for his services.

Mr Mason, having taken the chair, seconde3, and spoke in high terms of the valuable services Mr Pearson had rendered to the township as cha;rman of the Coun- cil. He also thanked the members for electing him RR chairman, and he expressed the hops that he would re- ceive the same support as Mr Pearson had. Mr. Clarke seconded the motion, which was heartily passed, and in reply Mr Pearson said he had consielere'd it to be an honour to have been chairman of the Parish Council of his native village.
THE OVERSEERS.

The next business was the election of overseers. The Clerk stated that Mr James Warburton declined to accept office again. Mr. Pearson propose th tt Mr. Clarke and Mr. Whitley be elected. Mr. Clarke said he bad not much time to devote to the duties of the office, and Mr Fairhurst having expressed his willingness to take the office, he and Ur. Whitley were appointel, a member remarking that they were both independent gentlemen with ample time at their disposal to carry out the duties.;

div.head: NEW RATE.--A DECREASE.
div.p: THE NEW RATE.--A DECREASE.

The clerk said it would be some satisfaction to the new overseers to know that the rates for the ensuing year would be a penny less than at present—(hear, hear),—and there was a fair balance in hand. In reply to a question, Mr. Bradshaw said the poor rate would be is id and the special rate 73 for the half-year, maisirie, 3s 4i for the year. The rat 33 had ben as high as 3s 10d.
A TIN BOX WANTED.

The Clerk was asked if tilers was any further busi- ness, and replied that he did not know that there was unless the Council cbon to buy him a tin b)z to keep the Council's books in. The Council thoinht the Clerk ought t) have a box, and it was resolved to buy 006 and have it suitably lettered.

div.head: BAD FOOTPATH.
div.p: A BAD FOOTPATH.

Mr. Whitley complained of We state of the footpath leading from Fairfield-road to Mill Pool. It was nigh time that some attention was given to it. Considerable dismission ensued as to who was respon- sible for its being kept in a good state, and it was decided to give notice to the parties concerned to have it put in proper order: ,Tlais concluded the business.

div.head: Annual Parish Meeting.
div.p: Annual Parish Meeting.

The annual parish meeting was held at the conclusion of the Parish C macil meeting. Mr. Mason presided.and there were also present MoS3rB Clarke. Pearson, Weitley, Mclntyre, Fairhurat,F Timperley. E England, McGregor Spencer, H Isherwood, and Bradshaw (clerk). The business was " to discuss parish affairs." Mr. Mclntyre was informed by the Clerk that this year there would be no Parish Council eiectiens. The present members rennainel in office another year.—la reply to Mr. Isher- wood, the Chairman said he did not think there was the I slightest hope of getting the hoardings at the Swing Bridge removed unless the weather came to their assis- tance. (Laughter.) Mr. Mclntyre remerk ,d that it was a pity the Parish Council could not air Inge for the March winds to blow all the year round in the vicinity of the hoardings.—The Chairman said he thought the hoardings would have been blown down during the gale on Good Friday.—Mr- England drew attention to the width of Waltoneread and asked if a build- ing line had been fixed. At present there seemed to be /self-a-dozen building lines.—The Chaii- = man said the Parochial Committee nad fixed the width of the road at 40 feet, and when it was built on br:r.h sides it would be found that the road would be that width, if not mere in parts.—Mr Isherwood mentioned that in the winter considerable inconvenience often re- sulted from the lamps being put out at midnight. He sugzested that the lamps at the Swing Bridge, V ctoria Square, London Bridge. and Walton-road should be left lighted all night.—The Chairman said the only objection was the expense which would be incurred.—Mr Pearson said the rate for light- ing was alresdy 211., and he did not think it wee policy to increase it. —Mr England gaid it was their pelicy to attract residents, and if the turning out of the lamps at midnight caused inconvenience he should be in favour of keeping a few lighted. He had heard numerous complaints from workmen who had to go to work early in the morning.—The Chairman said he would bring the matter before the Lighting sub-commit- tee of the Parnehial Committee.—The meeting closed with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: MYSTERIOUS CASE AT PENKETH.
div.p: A MYSTERIOUS CASE AT PENKETH.
Death in a Barn.

Mr. Brighouse, county cqroner, conducted an icquiry at rhe Crcwn Inn, Penk !tg, on Today morning, con- cerning the deith of an unknown min, which took place in a barn at Peuketh on Thurs lay mornin,q,

John Cain, lodging-house min'ager, 2, -Oxford-street, , Widnes, said he had known too deceased for two weeks. He cause to his house on the 3.d, aud stopped until the 11th. He (witness) only hew his name as !Lary." He had a melodeon, and evidently got his liring by playing it. Be was a matt who took a deal of drink and very little food. He (witliess) considered him to be a fairly healthy man. During toe eight days he was at witness's house he only know him to have one meal, and that was on Monday week, when he had SOMA mutton. He lert the house about four o'clock on the afternoon of tbe 11th, with a hawker and his wife, who had been at his house since the 7th, and the three appeared to be on the best of terms %hen they went away. He had heard deceasel say that he had it wile sal family in the north of England. His age was about 35 years. He had no money when ha left witness's_house. _

John Hueaphries, landlord of the Cuerdley Cross, Cuerdlee, sated that the deceased WAS in his house, on tne 11th and had two al4ssei of beer, tagether with the man and woman already m-ntioned. They were all perfectly sober and friendly when they left at nine o'clock. Deceased was playing a mei, dean in the house. John Fisher, carter, resi fliv, with his father at Mar- tinscroft Farm, Penketh, said tat at eleven o'c'aock on the night of the 11th he was di,turbed by the dog bark- ing. He got up and examine 1 the premises, but found no one. At e.le o'clock tho next morning he was called by his father, and to.-zether they examined the premises and found the deceased on some straw in the barn. He was quite naked. Witneps asked hnn hiw Ise came there, and he said be missed his way and came in for shelter. He was asked to leave but refused. They left him there, and about 7-30 witness again saw him standing up and shivering. Du:eased asked him if he had an o'd shirt to spare, and he replied that he had no. Ho did not com- plain about being ill, mai in answer to a question, re- garding the marks on his face deceased said he had been attacked and robbed. He was a sailor from Widnes. Witness did net see him alive again. P.C. Coupe, stationed at Ponk.,th, said he was called to the farm about nine o'clock and saw the deceased in a barn loft on same straw. He was then partially dressed. Qaestionel by witness he said be had missed his way and had gone into the barn for shelter. He was very cold and his clothes were wet through. Witness said he must not stay there' and the deceased asked him if be could warm himself at his cottage fire. Witness gave him permission, and said he would find him an old shirt.

When deceased came d )wn he sAemel to collapse, and witness going to his assiranhe found him to be very ill. Ho went into th 3 house fir sine warm tea, and on his return found that the man was deid. Deceased had not complained to him of hiving bean attacked, or id-used. He said he was a p-msinner in the army, and received 7d per day, having served 18 years. He htd drunk heavily, but on the previous day he had only had about two pinta. He was is slmpany with a man and woman, but he lost them. On hit was found a quantity ot blank cards and a melodeln was lying in the straw. The deceased was about 35 years of age and was about 51t 6in, in height.

Dr. Murray, Pen'teth, stated that he made a post ',torten examination of the deceased. Ile attribute the man's death to shock following pneumgnia and lace Mon of the right kidney. On the advice of the Coroner, the jury returned an open verdict.

div.p: LIVERPOOL COUNTY QUARTER
SESSIONS.

The business of the Liverpol County Quarter Session was clmonenced on Tuesday morning in the Session House. Islington, Sir William B Forwood presiding. The other magistrates prere7rt were Mcs4rl. John Formby, M F Burrows, J Hartley, W Rtehardson, .1 Handley, J Shaw, E Cannineton, G Go-rdison. a R Willis, J Lister, H %V Gair, G D Killry, C Sod, William Lees, hi'Clure. and T Comber.

div.head: 7A Dishonest Earlestown Domestic.
div.p: 7A Dishonest Earlestown Domestic.

Agnes Hudson (221, domestic servant, pleaded guilty to having btolen a gold breastpin, the property of Thos. Lytbgna. She pleaded not guilty to the theft of a cash- bag, five surer crushers, a bottle of whiskey and one of rum, and £42 6s lid in money, belonging to James Lvthgoc. Mr Rigby Swift con -laded the prosecution.— It appeared from the evidence that the prisoner,who was then in poor circumstances, was, in July last, engaged by James Lythgoe, licensee of the 0 ilfellows Arms, Earlestown, as a domestic slrvant at 22s per month. Shottly afterwards money was missed from the till, at the same time that the prisoner seemed to be flush of coin. On her boa being searched the articles named were found, along with £4.2, nearly all in small silver. In accounting icr her posseisiin of the money% the girl said that she had £35 on eatering upon t'se situation,and the elder Lythgoe gave her the remainder. The jury found the prisoner guilty, but recommended her to mercy on account of the temptation which access to the :ill had been to her. She wi: sent to prison for two months.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT VULCAN
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT VULCAN
FOUNDRY.
Inquest at Warrington.

Mr. S. Brighouse, county clroner, conducted an inquiry at the Police %.,tation, Warrington, on Tues- day afternoon relative to the death of John*Walsby of 127,Legh-street,garlestown.wlio died on the previ.. ous Friday evening at the Warrington Infirmary from injuries sustained whilst following his employment at the Vulcan Foundry,Newton-le-Willows.—Alajor Roe, one of /ler Majesty's Inspectors of Factories, watched the proceedings, and Sir. Richards, of the Vulcan Foundry Company,produced a sketch show- ing the operations in which tke deceased was engaged at the time of toe accident. The first witness called was Joeeph Dutton, of War- grave-road, Earlestown, who said the deceased was bid uncle and lived at 127, Legh-street, Earlestown. He was a bachelor, 58 years of a :e. and employed as a general labourer at Vulcan Foundry. The accident happened on Tiles lay, tne 27zh of March. He did not witness the occurrence but he believed the decessed and another man were at work lifting an iron cylinder when by some means the barrel of the cylinder fell on the deceaseci•d foat. He saw the deceased after the accident but be did not attach blame to anyone. Joseph Thompson, employed at the Vulcan Foundry, stated that on the date named they were taking an out- side cylinder off a drilling machine. The object was to turn the eylinder over. It was suspended by means of a sling, and when witness asked the deceased to take the sling off be placed one haud on the cylinder and that caused the barrel of the cylinder to drop on his left foot. The foot was released and the boot removed. The toe was badly crushed and the foot was covered with blood, the dee .ased was taken horns and on the 541 of the present month he was removed to the Warrington Infirmary• Nurse Rebinson stated that the deceased was admitted into the Warrington Infirmary on sth inst and died in her presence on th” 13h inst. The cause of death was due to a crushed foot and blood pokoning. The jury after a short consultation returned a verdict of " Accidental Death." The Coroner thanked Mr. Richards for his sketch which had greatly facilitated the inquiry.

no onne r Tuesday conductedon the Sudden Death at the Workhouse. e ci.Mure. aSt, . eSt rti hg eh o sal ice o usn body of a man unknown, who died at the Work- house last Friday.—Jehn Barnsley, Lingley Green Farm, Sankey, stated that the deceased was found in an exhausted condition in one of his fields be- hind a manure heap at six o'clock last Thursday evening. He was taken to the County Police Station.—Dr. G. Braide, visiting surgeon at the Warrington Workhouse Infirmary, stated that the Station i oc coroner, deceased, who was a foreigner about 42 years of age, slept in the tramp ward at the Workhouse on Wednesday night. On Thursday morning witness saw him when he was suffering from paralysis. He left the Workhouse on Thursday . and was brought back in on unconscious con- dition by the police. He was suffering from compression of the brain. Flo never regained con- zciousness and died on Friday night. On Wednes- day night whilst in the Workhouse he had a fall and injured his cheek. Witness had made a post mortern examination of the body and found signs of 1 extensive pleurisy. There were clots on the top of the brain between tbe brain and the membranes. This in itself was sufficient to account for the death. On dissecting the brain he found the whole of the right latteral ventricle was filled with a blood clot which would weigh about, three cparters of an ounce. The arteries at. the base of the brain were ruptured and weakened and the rupture of the arteries was the cause of the tlood clot.—ln answer to a member of the jury the doctor sai4 deceased was in a fit condition to leave the Workhouse.when witness saw hire. He spoke to the deceased but he could net tell what h said.—A verdict of death from natural causes was returned.
