Tun criticisms upon the Our Bad Spion Kop despatches, in Generalship. which approval is gener- ally expressed of Lard Roberts's censures, are the more remarkable in that they harmonise with Much that was said in this country at the time. Weed not go over them in detail. What the emlutry is most anxious to know is this—what is the true explanation of our bad generalship? The question opens up a variety of opinions, and weak Points are so numerous that they must command attention. War is a game in which many blunders 4e Constantly made, and some of the mistakes cilli4cle before Ladysmith have been charitably put ;Iva to the absence of good maps of that most Lfacult country lying between the Tugela and a.dYsraith. We are very much afraid that sovie- tht Mg more serious is revealed by the actions before 4dYarnith and the various reverses which our arms :Pe experienced. Oar generals seem to have been ilsalliting in proper training and skill, and t'eu we have cleared away all that is local and BMP°rary we come to the central truth of all—the lack of scientific training. Aldershot may not be a Ilgio.c"zi school, and probably we do not practise a llitarY manceavres often enoug,a, and on a scale Ilf4eient to train our superior officers. But the 41.8 t conantent is the one that has been often made 11(1 may recur several times before the war is .Over. The lessons learnt at Aldershot do not 'cieera to have been prattised in South Africa. rdinarY precautions have been neglected. The eci outing t has been bad, and the supply of informa- Zinmc"t imperfect. The night attacks have often made under careless conditions. Tae ad- The alliaVelclem been conducted in the right way. forml -:g`idaled Brigade ht in the wrong 1' °-- was caught surprised, and tunable to do what was urequiredn of it. Superficial preparations have cost Many valuable lives, and when the right moment calla° We have failed to take advantage of it. The Mishap to the guns at Colons° was due to an imperfect understanding of the order .t° be executed. The failure to push home tille attack on Modder River lost us a great chance, and the same may be said of the battle of Magersfontein. Bad scouting and loose 6rders lost us the guns at Koorn Spruit. Failure . 14) understand the real dangers to be faced lost us the companies surrounded at Raddersburg. We 'aye to deal with an alert enemy, full of tricks,and /31-1 r generals should meet trick with trick. The ?IcPerience gained against less civilised foes, with 411crior weapons, has invested the "luck and pluck', I,l3o,etriee with a fascination which seems irresist- tols• It makes our generals careless. The power b.,.act together, the readiness to assume responsi- -1114, the knowledge what to do in difficult seem to be conspicuous by their 18ence• The moral of it all is this—that our Iceets are not properly trained in the art of war. ° must add that they are not always rewarded With commands according to merit and experience. thh e Proposed inquiry into the administration of h: War Office must, accordingly, be so compre- a as to take in the whole subject of the train- -114 of °Lir officers, which events have proved to be arnentably deficient. We spend money enough ref. °lir army, and we do not get back an adequate for what we spend. Why we do not is the (1:11sne to be faced, and the country must make e413,,:ts mind to carry the thing through thoroughly, " to insist upon real and not sham army reform.

THE QUEEN'S example has been -The Queen's followed to a large extent this tecample. h Easter, and holiday-makers avi, 'eon staying at home, finding the change 4of creation they wanted within the compass tritish Isles. The more adventurous have 11-114 e to the Continent, as they will always do, ta. ether there are Exhibitions to visit or not, be- tll! they imagine that foreign scenes and foreign itit—i'er enlarge the experience and quicken the r) ertlect• Home attractions, however, are much -°,,chaveniently at hand, and they are suffi- th.i 'IY diversified to give men and women every- -4itnß they want. If they want the sea, it en- fikttlies us, and there are coast lines of every kind, the' l'QekY, bold, and pleasing. At this tinie of dailYear the sea is apt to be wild and stormy, etin'3rcm3 for boating and yachting,and not warm the -ugh for bathing. Later on, it will well reward all Ivill".ekers after pleasure and health,and its voice elok to the cadenceof Lake Leman in BYRON S 81;tilaCitabl6 verses ; it will " sound sweet, as if a fEtd:l'3 voice reproved," and" stern delights" may - before its entrancenaents. Tee mountain- :abets and hill-top people, who dislike the plains these calms, can always find plenty of work in of ": `slands without the diet and the discomfort 414nge lands, where the British-born are fi charged higher prices than other persons, and 47,ee(ei whenever opportunity offers. Wales lan the Lake District, Scotland and parts of Ire- 'cvlal,' k',4re 'lot to be despised, except by travellers „ esire to see snow in the summer, and to blo:ali" appalling landscape," as Mr. JOHN charms eXPreSses it. For lakes we can offer toi4d—sa that are sufficient for the moderate- to b e"' Iv" do not desire to dream on Como, or °reminded of the sea on Lake Wener. The

'British and Irish lakes are romantic and well worth a visit, and yet some of theta have never been visited by the persons whose first thought in holielay-making is to get away from the sound of their mother-tongue. Steamboat trips and coach- rides can be had in abundance in many parts of these islands. There are even woods and mcorlands, crags and valleys, for the seeker after pretty scenes, sketchy bits, and snap-shots, with a camera. For mere rest-seekers, who need fresh air, perfect repose, and good food, what can be better than a short time spent at a farm-house, away from the roar of traffic, the dust of cities, the excitements of war news and busy street-crossings ? The Queen has preferred to stay at home this year. She is in Ireland, and next month she will jour- ney to Scotland. She has drawn to Dublin many persons who might otherwise have been scamper- ing over the Continent or idling on the Riviera. Her example may very well be followed by her subjects. Many reasons exist why they should prefer to stay at home in their holiday-making this year. The pressure of the war will affect the purse, the sorr Ivy and pathos of it will touch the spirits, the politics of it will never cease to interest the mind. Whilst the war with Spain lasted the Americans preferred to stay at home. Let us do the same. Not to avoid danger *need we do this, but under the influence of feelings which draw us to our own kith and kin, which have made the British Isles the centre of so much of our thought and life, it will be better for us all, for the home health reiorts, for the unity of our families, and above all for our incomes and the Imperial Ex- chequer.

The cricket season will not be tne IeSS interest- ing because the Australians are absent. They are playing a gallant game in another field. Mean- while at home the counties can seriously devote themselves to the championship matches. It is probable that there will not be so much fresh blood in the field as was anticipated at the close of last season, and that is all to the good if the fresh blood is drawn from abroad' Last year a good deal of gossip about the qualification of leading. Australians for county cricket excited fears that the fine okt gams was going the way of football. Happily, gossip was a lying jade; but the pessi- mists did not paint the results too black had rumour been entirely vindicated. County cricket will cease to attract anything like the amount of interest at present centred upon it when counties are permitted to buy assistance from abro id. The star system is wanted by nobody. What many would like to see would be cricket played by men wholly born and bred in their county. The matches would increase in interest. A useful and praiseworthy pride in one's district would be fostered. Often it is said that the cricketers of to-day are degenerates, and unworthy to be com- pared with their ancestors in the game. There are two opinions about that. The game itself must and will degenerate when it can be said that victory is the appanage of the longest purse. Whera the financial factor has beau most completely elimina- ted rational interest is quickened and the game benefits.

It is said that had the Paris Exhibition been delayed another two months it would have been in no forwarder state. The firms who have entered for the various sections have the greatest reluctance to expose their goods while heavy traffic and unpacking is going on around, and, conse- quently, all delay to the last moment. The notice was, however, issued this week that nothing would he received after Tuesday next, and as no stock or waggon is allowed to enter the yard in the day time, while the visitors are about, a wonderful converging of stores occurs in the late hours of the night. Of course, it may be said that this final warning might have been issued a week before Easter, and have produced a good result; but the exhibitors know that the rich uying people will not arrive ' much before Whitsuntide, and they are anxious that the goods shall not lose their bloom or fresh- ness of paint. But the Parisians themselves do not grumble about this. The Exhibition is so varied that it is well perhaps to have it revealed in stages—at first the buildings, then the entertain- ments, next the wonders of art and mechanism,aud finally the educational sections. For the present the one-franc tickets of admission are being sold at the modified price of sixty centimes, and no one grudges sixpence for such a display as is already there. As for the English, the wise among them will hasten over before the end of June. Paris is always hotter than London in summer,and what will it be this year, with the crowding of sightseers ?

More trifling with the Standing Orders! We are horrified to learn that the salutory admonition administered to the Paving and Sewerage Com- mittee has not deterred the Town Hall, Park and Baths' Committee from treating the Standing IRrders with scsiat respect, and even levity. A fort- night ago, the committee advertised for tenders. for a painting contract, but not in one of the three recognised local newspapers. No ! the advertise- ment appeared instead in "Sunrise," to the com- plete and painful exclusion of the aforesaid local newspapers. We acquit " Sunrise "of any com- plicity in this terrible affair, and on enquiry the only person on whom we can lay the guilt seems to be the Chairman of the Committee, Alderman Bolton. The latter gentleman has some hazy notions of humour,and we believe it was with the idea of being funny that he caused the adver- tisement te appear in so unusual a place. Whether this extremely pondrousjoke was meant to be at the expense of the Mayor,the Standing Orders,the aforesaid papers, or even " Sunrise ' we do not profess to know. But as a sample of an aldermanic joke we can only look upon it with pain, and sad- ness inexpressible.

It is satisfactory to learn that the application of the Warrington Corporation for power to con- struct tramways within the Borough is likely to be granted by the Board of Trade. It took the Corporation a great number of years to make up its mind to adopt electricity but since a definite decision was arrived at, rapid progress has been made. By September next we have been prom • ised electric light and if the application for tram- ways is conceded we may expect within the short space of a few years to draw level with the most enterprising of munici- palities, in the working of electric tramways. It is unfortunate that Warrington should have so many "narrow places" along the route of the pro- posed tramways but one of the results of the in- troduction of this new means of locomotion may he the hastening of the work of widening the thoroughfares.

Whatever charge may be laid against the mem- bers of the Warrington Board of Guardians it cer- tainly cannot be said that they are afraid of spending money. At the meeting on Wednesday, Mr. J. W. Knowles was of an inquisitive turn of mind and asked to be informed of the little bill which the Guardians have run ou in connection with the new workhouse infirmary. The building is, of course, in an incomplete state, and it was therefore impossible to give a definite answer, but the questioner was informed that it was anticipated that this new home for the sick poor would he obtained for a mere £35,000. It was with little effect that Mr. Kuowles pleaded that the original estimate was £20,000, and he was given to understand that he must now devote his attention to yet another scheme of ex- tension at the Workhouse. This time it is for laundries, lavatories, ac., but it was deemed inad- visable to enter into details as to cost: In this respect the Guardians adopted a wise course, judg- ing by their previous experience of estimating the cost of extensions. The plans were approved and a few more thousands must now be added to the Guardians' little bill for improvements at the Workhouse.

div.p: THE EXAMINER, PRIDAY, APRIL 20, 1900.

with the winter game. Interest in the latter is, however, waning and people are beginning to look ahead to the premier summer pastime as the days grow warmer and "Old Sol's " beaming counten- ance breaks through the clouds with increasing frequency. It is very pleasing to note that the prospects of the County Palatine are particularly bright, for not only is the "new blood" unearthed last year still available together with "Johnny Briggs" and the regular players, but the team will have the great blessing of a permanent captain— aid he no less a person than Mr. A. C. Maclaren. Since Mr. A. N. Hornby's palmy days, the Lancashire eleven have been with- out a permanent "skipper," and the disadvantage of having this amateur or that in casual charge has been frequently made manifest. Mr. Maclaren is the beau ideal of what a captain should be, and as he has already captained "All England" he pos- sesses uncommon qualifications for the post of looking after the Lancastrians. As a batting side the team will be immensely strengthened by the presence of Mr. Maclaren in every encounter, and given ordinary luck in the matter of weather and other circumstances, the championship should this year be claimed on behalf of the Red Rose.

ST. PAUL'S WESLEY GUILD.

The Recreation Branch of the above Guild, held a social evening on Easter Monday in the Guild Par- kur, Brunswick school. Songs and solos were con- tributed by Miss liallding, Miss Carter, Mr H Dodd and Mr G R Johnson; a duet by Miss Carter and Mr G Pennington. and a reading by Mr J Barker. Supper was provided at 8.30 to which the company, numbering about 50, did full justice. A phonograph in charge of Mr G R Johnson created roars of laughter. The remainder of the evening was spent in parlour games, &c. The singing by tha wnole company, of' Auld Lang Syne "brought to a close, a most successful and enjoyable gathering.

div.head: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CYCLE CLUB.
div.p: RUNCORN WESLEYAN CYCLE CLUB.

This club, which has only just been reorganised for the season, had its first run on Monday last. The destination was Hawarden Castle, via.. Eaton Hall, and the outing proved highly enjoyable.—At the club meeting Mr. R Pavah was elected to the chair, and the following appointments were made : Messrs S Dutton, secretary; J 11 Jones, captain of the Wednesday section; George liayes, sub-cspLain; J Pickthall, captain of the Saturday section ; J Jones sub-captain. On Welnesda.y. the club run was to Delamere Forest, and favoured with fine weather, a goodly number started. SALE Or WORK AT THE MERSEY MISSION. The announcement appears in our advertising columns of a sale of work to be held in aid of the Seamen's Institute, Station-road, Runcern. on Wed- nesday and Thursday, April 25th and 26th, 1900. The object of the venture ts to raise funds to clean, paint, and ventilate the church and institute. Lady Brooke, will open the proceedings the first day, and Miss Naylor, of Thelwall, the sec )nd day. There willalso be a children's day on the Priddy. when the opening ceremony will be performed by Mrs. Stokes. of Rock Savage. The work of the mission is one that commends itself to the public gener- ally, and should receive unanimous support on account of its cosmopolitan character. For further particulars see advertisement. LUNCH BASKET AND SOCIAL AT RUNCORN.

A diversion took place at the Mersey Mission, on Tuesday last, when a lunch basket sale and social evening took the place of the weekly concert. There was a fair attendance. Owing to the un- avoidable absencs of Mr George Duckett, M.r W Shaw (junior),offerad the lunch baskets by mock auction, and they changed hands at a good figure. They were contributed by Mrs Briscoe and sirs Young (double basket), Misses L and Fiorrie Shaw (double basket), Mrs Ashcroft and Mrs Hughes (single baskets.) Previous to the sale songs were rendered by Misses Garvie, and M fill and Messrs. James Shaw, John Hart (a sailor), and Master Frank Rodgers. of the ship "Duchalburn." Mr W Byfield also contributed several records upon his gramaphone. The remain- ing portion of the evening was spent in parlour games. Miss Garvie was the accompanist. RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS.

At the Runcorn Petty Bessions, on Tuesday morn- ing, there was but little business of interest. The presiding magistrate was Mr. F. Wiswall,—Frank Norman NlcLeod, ani James Gorman, sailors, were each tined 5s or 83 61 costs or an alternative of 7 days hard labour, for being drunk in the streets on the 14th and 16th instants respectively.—Wil- liam Johnson, Thomas Walsh, and James Gavon, ol no address, were charged with begging in Church- street, on the previous day (Easter Monday).—Act- ing Sergeant Gregory stated he saw the prisoners. Johnson was in the middle of the road, and the other two on the road side. Walsh asked witness, who was in plain clothes, for a copper, but he re- fused him. Witness then went and got the assist- ance of P.C. Carrington and arrested the three prisoners whom they found in the "George Inn" with a quart of beer before them. On being put into the cells, Johnson used most abusive languags. in fact, in all his previous experience witness had never heard the like.—Walsh, for the defence, denied that he asked Gregory for a copper. He only asked for a "pipe of bacca."—The trio were committed to !Kuutsford for 7 days hard labour. SONS OF TEMPERANCE,. RUNCORN.

_ The fortnightly meeting of ibis order was held on Saturday evening in the Greenway-road school. Mr Thomas R. Whyte occupied the chair. After the routine business had been transacted, Mr Thos. Cooke, one of the auditors, read the report,in which he pointed out that the cadets had been very for- tunate in having little sickness during the quarter. Eight new members had joined, making a total of 114, after having transferred a number to the adult order. They now had .£ll6 13s 51 in hand. ía the adult order there were 311 m-snabers, and they had paid for sickness and accidents £Bl 13s 61 to 61 members. During the quarter one member and a member's wife had been removed by death. There was a discussion on the report in which the follow- ing officers took part :—.Messrs James Johnson, Thomas J Holt, and Daniel 13isbrown. On the motion of Mr Thomas Clarke, seconded by Mr Thomas Heesom, the report was unanimously adopted. An interesting meeting then terminated.
INFLUENZA CA.TJSES A WIDNES MAN TO HANG HIMSELF.

Llst Saturday morning, a young man named Edwaid Walton, aged 27 years, residing at 136, Mersey-road, Widnes, checker, employed by the London and North Western Railway, was found dead hanging from a beam in the wash-house. The deceased had suffered from influenza and bad been attended by D. Hutchinson: On Friday he com- plained of pains in the head. About ten o'c:ock in the evening he, his wife, and two children retired to bed. Deceased got up at five o'clock on Saturday morning to attend one or the children who was ill. He afterwards went to bed again. About 6-30 Mrs. Walton awoke and missed her husband. She at once dressed and want downstairs in search of him. Upon going into the wash-house in the yard she found him as described. A man named Starkey cut the man down, and it was found that life was ex- tinct. The police were notified, and they have for- warded the circumstances on to the Coroner.

The Compensation for the Loss of an Eye. At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before His Honour Judge James, an application was made by Mr. Payne, of the firm of Messrs Payne. Galloway. and Payne. of qanchester, on behalf of Messrs. Joseph erosfield and Sons, Limited, for a review under the Workmen's Compensation Act of an awasd r, 124 6d per week made by His Honour Judg,-, Wynne Ffoulkes in favour of Patrick Tanian, formerly a Caustic labourer in their employ, as com- pensation for the loss of his right eye.—Mr Forshaw represented the defendant.--Mr. Payne stated that he proposed to show that the amount awarded of 12s 61 per week was more than the respondent. was entitled to under the Acr, and that he was prohibi- ted from proving the sum at the arbitration owing to the firm's default in filing an answer. i.elied solely ou section 12 of schedule 1 as sup- porting his application for a review.— ND.. Forshaw submitted that his Honour could not go behind the order which had been made. To enable the firm to review the order it was necessary that the circum- stances should be altered. There was no evidence that any alteration of circumstances had taken place since the order was made.—His Honour said he could imagine that where misleading evidence had been given it was possible for the Court to look behind the judgment.—Mr. Forshaw stated that the 128 61 award was assessed on an average earning of 30s a week.—Mr. Payne said be was prepared to prove that the wages of the respondent did not average that amount.—A.fter further discussion the case was adjourned by consent matil May 31st.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT UOUNCIL.
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DIS- TRICT UOUNCIL.
ANNUAL MEETING. -- Election of Chairman and Committees.

Tha annual meeting of the Runcorn Urban Die- trict Council was held at the Town Hall on Thurs- day morning, when there were present :—Messrs Wiswall (presiding), S Taylor, W Handley, h Imi- son, J W Lightburn, H G (i.rice,E Gatley, S Walton, I' Dean, J Wilson, R H Posnett, T Jones, J II Sal- keld, D Bisbrown, with E Marshall (secretary),P A Lake (law clerk), and James Wilding (surveyor).
THE ELECTION OF CHAIRMAN.

Mr. F. Wiswall, the tet.ring cnauensu, iutimatei teat the first business was the election of chairman. He had great pleasure therefore in moving that Mr W Handley be thee' next chairman. He had every reason to believe that the nomination would receive the unanimous sup- port and vote of the whole chamb ir. Personally he was cordially in support of it and wished Mr Rendley a most successful year of office if elected. Mr Lia.udny, he felt sure, would do credit to the office and would do every- thing to uphold the houolir sad dignity of the Council. Wear, hear.) Alf d Taylor had much pleasure in seconding the election of Mr Handley whom be felt was eminently fitted for the position. Mr. Headley had taken a very active part in every branch of work which had for it end the good of the town and the good of tne towns- people. (Hear, hear.) He was one of tiseir oldest members and had been a member of the B iard ot Cone snis.sioners for several years. Ho was sure as the chair- man had put it that Mr Handley wsuld de every credit to the Council and also to the town. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Imisou supported the proposition. Mr. Handley was perhaps, he said, the oldest public servant they had in Runcorn. One of his (Mr. Imison's) recollections wa of Mr. Handley as a public man, and he used to be rather inclined to take him as his model. He had not been quite so much inclined of later years, but he had always felt that whatever Mr. Handley undertook he did thoroughly and to the best of hi 3 conscience and ability, and in chat respect he was second to none. There were many points of difference between Mr. Handley and himself, which would perhaps exist as long as they were there, but in Mr. elandley they had a man who would conduct the affairs of the Council in a business- like way, and a man ef whom they would all be proud whenever ho had to represent them in any official capacity. He was sure Mr Wiswall had correctly inter- preted the desires and wishes of the Council in a letting that Mr. Handley would have a very happy year. Mr. R. H. Posenett, said when he entered the room that morning he had no idea that Mr Ha.ndley's name would be broeght forward as their future chairman. But as it had been he had the greatest possible plea-iure in supporting the election. If only for his encycle- pedrioel knowledge ef the town, and its history past and present, there was no one who could stand near him. ( Hoer, hear.) In everything connected with the town Mr. Handley had shown a very deep interest indeed. The Cheirman teen put the resolution which was unanimously agreed to. Subsequently ha vacated his seat in which he duly in- stalled Mr. Handley as his successor, investing him with the chain of office and saying, he had great pleasure in announcing him the duly elected Chairman of the Oouncil. (Applause.) Mr. Handley, now took the chair,and in a voice which betrayed considerable emotion, delivered a brief speece. Ile said there were occasions when silence was most x pressiee of gratitude, and if it were right that was the course he would have teken that morning, but he could not forebear expressing to the members the great honour he felt he was having conferred upon him in reeeiviug this mask of their confidence at their heads. [tie honour he felt to be the greater because it had been so heartily proposed—with far too kind words—by Mr. Wiswall, Mr Taylor, Mr Imison, (whose father was one ' of his warmest friends) and Mr Posnett. To these gentlemen he felt indebted for their idol words, and he was very much indebted to the whole of the members for the unanimous vote with which they had endorsed the propesiti Looking back over well nigh half a ceatury—that was the existence of the Board of Commissioners and tee Council, for he could only reckon them as one—he was reminded that a number of worthy men had occupied the chair—ptominent townsmen who had been properly called the makers of Runcorn. And while he remem- bered those names he also remembered that their associa- tion with the Ciuncil added very much to the dignity and responsibility of those who were called upon to occupy tee chair. He only trusted that he might as worthily uphold its traditions as they did in their day. He would do his best, and •he could not , de more. It had been a distinguishing feature of tee members of the Council that they have al ways loyalty supported their chairman, and as he looked round the room, he felt satisfied he would be loyally supported in the year upon which they had now entered and that knowledge would make the duties of the offi -e not only pleasing but lighter than they otherwise would be. He therefore looked forward to having a very happy year and specially seeing that Runcorn had taken an upward leap and was now on the progressive grade alter a de- pressing period. He again thanked the members for coaferring upon him what he considered the greatest honour that could be paid to a townsman, and in conclusion proposed that a very cordial vote of thaaks be accorded th gr. Wiswall for his services dur- ing the past year, and that he be elected vice-chairman. On very few occasions had Mr. Wiswall been ablent from the meetings, and he had tried to do his duty faith- fully and fearlessly. Mr. Dean seconded the motion which was supported by Mr Bisbrown, Mr S Taylor, Mr Grice and Mr E Imieon. and unanimously agreed to. Mr. Wiswall in accepting the office and the vote of , thanks for past services, said he would like to review just a little, some of the work accomplished by the Council, whilst he was in office and whilst he had been la member of the Council especially so seeing the grumbling and pin-pricks that the Council was con- tinually called upon to bear. Taking the committeee,who could deny—though it was denied, but not truthfully— that the Highways and Buildings Committee had put tee roads into better condition. Indeed, if it was possible for the stones to cry out there would be an earthquake or something of that nature in Penmaennsawr. (Laugh- ter) With regard to sewerage also they had not only I provided the necessary services, but they had remedied other defective old ones. (Hear, hear.) With regard to the Health Committee who could deny that good had not been done by that Committee. (Hear, hear.) Those things all cost money and they could not do it without rates—but as regards the rates of the town, it could not be that they were frightening peoi le away. for he believed there were about 500 workingmen from Widnes who resided in Runcorn. That proved that Run- I *ern was a residential town. (Hear, hear.) Then again as Mr. Liaison and Mr. Lightburn had shown the empty houses in the town were getting gradually filled. Referring to the over-draft of which Mr. Wis- wall considered so much had been said of late, ha thought it was making great of little. As to the way in which the work of the Council had been done during the past it had been well done,though there were plenty who talked of it in a disparaging way. He stood there, however, to uphold the work of the Couneil land all its doings during his year of office, and as the ICouncil had stood by hint so would he stand by it. (Hear, hear.) He thanked them all for the support and guidance he had received during his year of office, and wished to testify his appreciation of the latest honour they had conferred upon bim by appointing him as vice-chairman. He was glad to receive their thanks which he took as a very great return for what he had been able to dn. (Hear, hear.) Whilst speaking he would like to compliment the officials of the Council for the very excellent manner in which they discharged their duties. He thought they should not miss the oppor- tunity of giving the officials credit for doing their work so thoroughly, eepelally in the face of the grumbling and pin pricks he had already referred to. (H ntr, hear.) In conclusion he aeain thanked them for the way in which they had spoken of himself.

div.head: Warrington Parish Church.
div.p: Warrington Parish Church.

The Rector (Rev. Canon Willis) presided at the annual vestry meeting of the Parish Church held in the National Soboolroom, Church-streq, on Tuesday evening. There were also on th• platform, Mr Craik and Mr Dewhurst (wardens) and Mr E A White (deputy vestry clerk). The clergy present were the Rev A S Cameron, MA., Rev F White B A.., mid the Rev G W Dickinson. BA. _ _ _

Mr John Dewhutst (people's warden) presented the accounts for last year—January Ist to December 31st. The ordinary offertories were £291 3s 21, and special £202 111 81, or a total of £493 143 101. Other receipts amounted to £lB7 17s 9J, making a grand total of re- c3!pts of £6Bl 1.2 s 7d. At the he4isming of the nrevi6us year they owe .1 Parr's Bank £2O 2s 6i. The total pay- ments were £683 175 Ed thus reducing the debt owing to the bank to £2 5s id. (Applause.) In comparing the figures with those of previous yesrs, Mr. Dswhurst showed that solid progress had been made. In con- clusion,he stated that the wardens had worked hartnonc ously together. He was sure Mr. Craik's whole heart was in the work. (Hear. hear.) Councillor S Davies moved the adoption of the report, and acknowledged the able way in which Mr. Dewhurst had presented the accounts. It was a satisfaction to know that the church was practically out of debt. There were certain things it was necessary to do, itivo'vi la an exoense of £3OO or more. Tho most imp ,rtant was the repair of the tower and spire. This work ought to be taken up at encl. He ventured to ask the parishioners to consider the wislom of some systematic or regular giving for church expenses. Care should he takm that the church offertories did not come under £lO a Sunday. Votes of thanks weze accordcd to the churchwardens, sithstnen, and auditors for th3ir servics during the past year.
A vote of thank' was also paased to the ladies for their services in tue parish during the pist year on the proposition of Mr T MR9OO, who proposJl it for the seventh year in succession.

Mr. Atkin, in a few well-chosen words propo,ed a vote of thanks to the assistant clergy.—Mr. Craik seconded and No prop4sition was unanimously csrrei. —The Rev A S Carnerou replied. Mr. Craik, in proposine a vote of thar.ks to the Rector for presiiing,stated that the affairs of the church were in a very heattoly state. At the present time they had a cre lit btlance in their favour of about £6O. (Applause). Tney were desirous of cleaning the interior of the church and also restoring the ornamental work over the west door. But this work could not be elm- menced until they had a larger balance in hand. With respect to the restoration et the spire there had not ben a fibersl response to the circulars which were sent out, and he was not in favour of commencing a work of that kind until the funds were forthcorning.—Mr. Dew- burst seconded the vote of thanks which was agreed to. The Rector, in acknowlecling the compliment, said he was anxious to make use of the site which had bmn nresented to triem Uy C)Ionel Blackburn% on Manches- ter-real. It would be necessary to spend between £2OOO and £3OOO in buildings. Re made mention of the fact now in order that they might bear the matter in mind. Colonel Blackburn° was anxious that some provision should be made for the spiritual wants of the people in that neighbourhood. The 'meeting. then terminated. St. Thomas's Stockton Heath.

rho Vicar (Rev. El V Pig,ot) presided over the annul vestry meeting in connection with this ptrish. There were alio present:—Xlessrs.Wiliiam Richardson (churcn- warden), JA McGregor, Srmuel Norbury, T J Lee, A Down, T Jackson, F Rose, F Timperley, and Spencif (clerk).
A letter of ap)logy for non-attenda,ncrl was road by tta Chairman trom Mr. fl•)bert Da7iel, wha said be was confined to the Uwe, suffering from au attack of rheu- matism.
FINANCIAL.

Mr. Richardson submitted the; annual statement of accounts. Among the items of receit.ts were—General offertory, £174 7a ; special offvitories, £69 131 10f i; the total receipts being £2BB 03 41. The general offertory was £Z6 17s 7d more toan last year, and the spcial off rtories £1 15s 2jl. The debit balance had been re- duced from £l7 to £B. They had a beautiful church, an excellent choir, and their cervices were very well rendered. He thought the congregations should sub- beribe to pay the whole expenses. The evening collecions, he was sorry to sav, were at times hardly sufficient to pay for the gas and coke, the average sum being 275. Mr. Ja.oksmi aitred if they could not have a more econemical way of lighting the church.

Mr. Richardson replied that they could. They were thinking of introducing, the inc ndescent light, but no- thing definite had yet been done in the matter. On the proposition of Mr. Pearson, seconded by Mr. Timperley, the accounts were passed. ELECTION OF WARDENS, lac. The Chairman regretted that Mr E W Woods declined to be nominated again as vicar's warder, and he woul I therefore nominate Mr Henry Greenall. annual vestry tneetinz in connection with the above church, wa held on Tuesday evening, the Rev E C E Carleton (vicar) presiding. FINANCIAL.

Mr. Forahaw presented the balance-het, which showed that the receints amounted to £327 149 21, and the expenditure to £324 13s. The receipts were £35 more than last year. The Chairman said that during the year they had not bad a collection for the Additional Curates' Society. The grant from this society, which was £4O, had not been received, for they had not had a curate, but a Sunday helper in Mr Carter, who was on 3 of the masers of the Manchester Grammar School. The services of this gentleman were greatly appreciated by the parishioners, and they desired to continue his services. He pointed out that as there was a new bishop, it was their duty to welcome him, and when ay appeal came from him, they must respond to it. He bad no doubt that they would do this, as it would be far to the benefit of the Church and God's Kinvdem. The Chairman, continuing, said that the accounts of the Weedall's Charity had been prepared by Mr. Rowsou, audited by Mr. Welsby, and paid. The Wm received wxa £ll 189 IA for the year and there was now a balance in hand of 8s id.
The accounts were passed, on the motion of Mr. White, seconded by Mr. Dunbabin.
OFFICERS.

The Chairman re-appeinted Mr. Forshaw as vicar's warden, and Mr. Halton was re-elected people's warden. Mr. Forshaw nominated Mr. Welslay as his sidesman, and • Mr. Halton nominated Mr. Dunbabin. The follow- ing were elected sidesmen :—Messrs. Rowson, Rose James Harding, Gsrrard.lledge. Cox, White, Dyke.H Naylor, Hunt, Joseph Hesketh, and John Harding. Mr Westbrook and Mr.Rowson were re-elected lay delegates, Mr. GF F White was re-elected vestry clerk, and Mr. Harrison auditor.
The Chairman proposed, and Mr. Rowslo seconded, a vote of thanks to the churchwardens, and a v,4te of thanks was also passed to tho chairman on the motion of Mr. Forshaw, sec•inied by Mr. Halton. _

The Vicar on behalf of the congregition tenth red the churchwardens (Massrs H U lirelherton had A Owen) their heartiest thanks for the services rendered by them during the past year. Mr. Armstrong se,...onded. and said that the wardens had done their dutv to the best of their ability and had given general satisfaction. The motion was carried unanimously and Mr. Brother- ton briefly responded on behalf of himself and Mr. Owen.
Thn Vicar then Nominated Mr. Arthur Owen as his warden far the coming year. _

expect to keep the church in a proper sae if they did not contributr. Be did not think thy people were quite so poor that they could not keep the church out of debt; A very slight increase in subscripinons would have paid the £5 and they bad had a fortnight longer this year than usual.

The Chairman sail that if the majority gave like the few, the income would be mora than doubled. The accounts were passed. A vote of thanks cv...s accorded to Mr. Herbert Wood, the deputy clerk, for his s,rvices.
THE LATE
itEV. P. J. BY!..

F Taylor, seconded by Mr Armstrong, it was decided that art expression of sympathy and con iolence with Mrs. Byrne on the death of her husband, the Rev P J Byrne, late curate at St. Ann's, be recorded on the minutes. div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES
THE DANGER OF PLAYING FOOTBALL IN THE STREETS.

At the Warrington Police Ce.art on Turstay, beforo Mesa. Birchail (in the chair), and S Wrigtit, William Jonnson. 31, Gololrae-street,Tnomas Ellison ani Elwin Ellison, of 6. Facccr.7-yard, were summoned fsr playing foatbali in Camnria Pace, on April B:h.—They pleaded pot guilty.—Henry Clare, bird dealer, 1, Flag-lane, stated that at two o'clock on the date in question (Sun- day), his attention was call d to the defendants, who, in company with others Were playing football in Cambria Place. Three halls came over bis yard wall that morn- ing. A woolen on, hit his dauzliter on the head. Defendants pinyed looltall from daylight un'il night.— P.C. Dennett stated that lin went to Cambria Place and the ball produced was kicked and dropped at his feet.—Deferniants said they were playing at rounders.— The Chief Constable red a letter which he had re- ceived from the Superintendent of the Nursing Ass,icia- ticn aaking that stringent meaeures might be taken to check lens who peridated in playing football in the stre€ ta. On Saturday morninz one of the nurses was knocked eff her bicycle, a new one, by a gang of youths in New-road. Heedless of her ball or her shouts they ran into her with such force that she and her bietce were thrown to the ground. escaping as by a miracle from being tlirown under a passinz 'bus. —The police were doing all in their now3r to put font- balling in the streets down —rho Cnairman remarked that foottail seemed to have taken possession of youths. —The Chief Constable It is th.ir religion now.—Mr. Birunall; It is a pity that a noble game in itself should be so made ro endanger eublic safety.—Detendants were each fined ss.

STEALING A BICYCLY,.—A. LAW STUDENT IN TROUBLE At the Warri ,gton P >lice Ceurt, on Thursday, betore Mr. John Pali clouvh (in the chair) and Mr. J Hepherd, Septirnus Warren Sherratt, a respectably dressed man, was chargcd ov,t". steeling from outside the saleroom of Robert Lowe, 1 Back-itree, at 5.45 the previous after- noon a gent's safety bicycle value £l2.—He nle.ded guilty.—Mr Unsworth, solicitor, arpsared on te.-Alf of She prosecutors, anti said that at 545 en Wednesday afternoon a woman came inte Mr Lowe's saleroom and told Mr. Lowe that a man had taken his bicycle which he had left at the isor. He went out and saw the prisoner Walking down Bank-street with the bicycle. He shouted to the man to stop and he did so. Prosecutor asked him what he was doing with the machine, and piisoner used impudence to him. Mr Lewe told him to go away arid he rfused. Prison,T was under the iuff- ence of drink, and at last Mr. Lowe sent for a colstable. Pri.oner was impudent to the °tit:7r and he was taksn into custody. It appeared that prisoaer was seen by two women pretending to read the notice in the saleroom window and presently he went off with the bicycle. The women remonstrated with him but ha would not take any notice. Pris-mer had up till lately been a respectable man and was a law studeat. Ho said he had given way to drink ls.ttly and came to Warramsten on the spree and did not know what he was doing. Mr: Lowe had he desire to press the case.— Prisoner said he was helples,l; drunk or he would not have done such an idiotic thing.—The Chief Constab;e said priconer had been in the town since November. He admitted to him last night that he had done nothing but drink the whole of that time. He was a law student but had beer, in had company for some time, and was living in a common lodging house. He was not help- lessly drunk by any means. During the list few months a number of bicycles had been lost in the town under similar circumstances —Prisoner said he came from Birkenhead. His father had been three times Mayor of Wrexham.—The Chairman said the prisoner was liable to six months imprisonment but the bench were'going to take a lenient view in the case in the hope that he would reform. If he would sign the pledge they would • order him to be imprisoned for three days as a caution. —Prisoner promised to sign the pledge.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
Worrlngton Borough Court.

MOND/X.—Before the Mayor (in tbe chair), Mr. T. Birchall, aud Mr. F. Monks. DETRIUDING THZ RAILWAY COMPANY.—Juseph Herbert was charged with traveling on taa Cheshire Lines Railway from Liverpool to Warrington on Saturday without previ- ously paying the fare with intent to avoid payment.—Mr. Winters, wh, appeared on behalf of the Cheshire Lines Committee said that the prisoner arrived at Warrington by the 7.30 train frorn Liverpool. He got out of the compart- ment and after V•rs tickets had been colleetei he was seen to jump in again just as the train was moving off. He was pulled out and he said he had no money and wanted to get to Manohester.—A line of 10s was imposed. •

TUESDLY.L-BefOre Messre T. Birehall (la the chair) and S. Wright, " A. REGULLII ROADSIR "—John Galll'ord, last from Wigan, whom the Chief Constable described as being a regular roadster was committed to gaol for 14 days with hard labour for begging in Dudley-street at 4.15 on Monday after- noon. IHE CHARGP: AG 411stil. SEACOMBZ FOOTBALLER..—George Stephenson, John Keenan arid Charles Henry Ord, of Sea- combs were charged with committing a breach of the peace by acting in a disorderly manner in Bridge street and Horsemerket-street on 31 itch 31st.—The Chief Constable said that the men were summoned to appear along with three other men last Monday but they thought fit to ignore the summons and did not appear. It was at first intended to issue warrAnts, but subsequently the more merciful view pre- vailed, and the defendanta were notified by the Clerk that they must Appear that day. Oct the 31st March the Seacomba Swifts football c üb. of which defendants were memberd, had been pleyif,g a match against a Warrington club and came off victorione. To celebrate the victory they acted like mad men in the streete, and though cautioned by the police they dentinal to desist, and had to be taken into custody. Their names were taken and summonses were issued.—P.C.'s Leoaard, Pennington and Clough, and Inspector Hackett gave evidence to the effect that defendants were jostling people and shouting and singing.—Ord, who pleaded not guilty, stated that he and Stephenson were thirty yards behind the other men. When the others were arrested they followed them to the Police Station to see if they co aid do anything for them.-1 he magistrates decided to deal with the defeedants in the same manner as they did with the other men, and bowed them over te keep toe peace and ordered them to pay the ees:.s which amounted to 108. Turner corroborated.—Tho Chief Constable sail the defendant had been before the Court eight times for various offences. He considered that to be an exceedingly bad case. The police had been unable to obtain the names of any of the others.—Defendant who denied the off ance and behaved in a very insolent manner In the dock was fined 23s and costs (21 8s Od in all) with the alternative of a month's imprisonment. ILLTRELTING A Cow —William Mannion, Hatton's Farm, Padgate, was summoned br cruelly Illtreating a caw by beat- ing it on the 6th inst.—He pleaded not guilty.—P.O. Delahay said he saw the defendant driving the cow in Churce Street. He struck it several times across the nose and head with a long stick without any provocation. Subsequently he saw him driving it in Alanehester-road and defendant struck it several blows about the body as hard as he could strike.— Inspector Browne of the Ft.S.P.C.A.. said he examined the cow at about 4 o'clock the same afternoon. It was an aged animal in poor condition being almost skin and bone. It was then in a state of exhaustion not having recovered from the knocking about. He spoke to the defendant and he Bald he gav3 it a "clout or two" because it ran up an entry near Bank Quay Bridge. —Defendant's employer stated that he had never known the defendant to illtreat any of his animals. Defendant was fined in the costs (55.)

PREMIER CYCLES price -29 173 63.--J. B. GARLAND, Cycle Factor, Bridge-street. Warrington. Sudden Death of a Warrington Coachman. Information was received in Warrington on Saturday, of the death of Mr. William Bradford,who for many years had been coachman in the employ of Mr. J. C. Sutton, Clerk to the Warrington Board of Guardians. It appears that deceased. in company with a friend, had journeyed to Manchester on Good Friday with a view of inspecting the docks. Returning homP, he arrived at the Central Station, Manchester, when he was suddenly seized with ill- ness, and despite medical attention expired in a few minutes. . Deceased was well-known in Warrington and di,trict, and was about 70 years of age.

St. Mary's Amateur Dramatic Society.

Performances of Boncicault's "Glrimaldt" were g ven ill St. Mary's Hall on Monday and Tuesday e ening,s by the St. Mary's Amateur Dramatic Sooiety in aid of the funds of the Catholic Associa- tion. The play was admirably presented being ex- cellently mounted and =staged. Of the principal characters Miss Nora' Flaming, as Violet scored a distinct success by her natural impersonation. As Julia Miss Burrows acquitted herself vary credit- ably. Mr. W Kilduff's Grimaldi was worthy of the highest praise. The stage managers were Messre. W and L Burrows. An orchestra, under the con- ductorship of Mr li Eccles, played selections of music during the intervals. Mr W Kilduff was an effilient hon manager, and Alessrs. J Mather and M 0 Hearne, satisfactorily discharged the secretarial duties.

Violent Assault on the Police at Haydock. At tha Newton Petty Sessions, last Thursday before Messrs T J Gillespie, J L Wood, R Stone,and C B F Borron, James Durkin was charged on a war- rant with assaulting P.C.'s liagger and Holmes at Haydock, on the 18th November, 1899.—Evidence was given to the effect that the prisoner and several other men were reported by the Con- s'ables for committing a breach of the peace. They assaulted the officers by kicking and otherwise ill- treating them. Some men came up and commenced to belabour the policemen and some other constables who had come to their assistance, with pokers and shovels and in the struggle Durkin escaped. The other men were brought before the magistrates and sentenced to terms of imprisonment.—Dr. Cobben, stated that he visited the Police Station on the 19th I\ovember and examined P.C.'s Holmes; and Dagger. P.C. Holmes had bruised wounds on the lip, bruises on the back of the l,,ft ear, bruises under the left eye, and several smaller bruises about the head,f ace and the shins. He was alio suffering from sickness. Witness concluded that he had been subjected to great violence. P.C. Dag ,er was suffering from bruises on the right cheek in front of the right ear. He said they had caused insensibility. There were several scratches on the face —Prisoner was com- mitted to gaol far three moaths. LADIBS BENT GLXCH BOOTS vim SHOBS UNDBR THE CLOCK. Warrington and Bank Quay Sailing Club. The opening of this season's racing, in connection with the above club, was carried out very succeas- fully on Saturday. The programme was as follows: —First, the yacht race, the course being from Widnes, round a buoy moored near Walton Arches, and back again to Vie east end of Messrs Monks, Hall and Company's old wall. The competing yachts and owners, were : The Connie, 15ft., J Gleave ; Not AU° wed, 16fr., F Turner; Nymph, 16ft., Messrs R and 11 Burthem ; Peggy, 18ft.. E Gallon ; Wild- flower, 221 ft., H Warburton. Handicap start, half- minute per foot. The race, which took place under very favourable conditions,there being a fine breeze and plenty of water,was won by the Nymph, Peggy being second. and Wildthwer third. The Connie was going well for second position, but when about 400 yards from the winning post she capsized. The crew were picked up by a boat near to,and escaped with a good wetting. The second event was a model yacht race, course 400 yards ; handicap start, one yard per inch length measurement. The yachts and owners were : Fairplay, Mt. lin., G Bell ; Albert, 3ft 14in., .1 Gleave ; Fairy, Mt. 21n., Messrs R and U Burthern ; and the Lilly, 4rt. sin., E Jack- son. The Fairy gained the lead soon after the start and won easily; the Lilly being second, and Albert third.
PUBLIC BENEFIT UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST OOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. The Warrington Equalised District Branch
Order of Druids, Mersey Lodge.

The members of this branch had a picnic to Altrincham on Saturday in commemoration of their first anniversary of the lodge. Before starting on their journey they had the satisfaction of inviting D.C.S.D. Houghton who accompanied them for the special purpose of making a presentation of a framed emblem of merit to Bro. John T. Lomax, secretary ef the lodge, for his valuable and energe- tic services in promoting the interest and welfare of the Order. He was accompanied by the D.G.M. and , as many of the district officers as could make it convenient to be present. The D.C.S. in making the presention, spoke of the pleasure it gave him to be present on that occasion and in handing over the Emblem of Merit to Bro. Lomax he said that gentleman was highly honoured in receiving this token of esteem and re- spect from his Bros. in general. He hoped and truste I Bro. Lomax would always be able to look upon it and say what a blessing it was to him when he took upon himself to become a member of the Order of Druids. Bro. Lomax responded. He thanked them for their kind appreciation of his services and at the same time hoped it would always be in his power to be of some use to the lodge. Speeches were made by D.G.M.C. Bebbington, Bros. Poaley, Oxley, Whitfield, Rigbey and Wilson who spoke of the progress of the lodge since Bro Lomax became the secretary. The presentation over, the party proceeded to the Wheat Sheaf, Altrincham, where a splendid spread was provided. After a look through the village the members returned to the Bridge Inn, Warrington, and finished an enjoy- able outing by having a little harmony amongst them 4elvee. Songe were sung by Bro G Rigbey, Bro Wilson. and Bro Tranter, At the Close the 'members joined hands and sang "Auld Lang Syne."

MAMMA: "What are you playing with, dark ling ?" Darling: "With a caterpillar and two little kittenpillars." Timm are more people cross-eyed in the tongue than in the eyes; they talk one way while they are thinking the other. AN old salt, sitting on a wharf, very soberly remarked, "I began the world with nothing, and I have held my own ever since." "I SUSPECT there has been some crooked work going on here," he said. And he was right. His wife had been driving nails. YOUNG WIFE (proudly) : "George always says there's no cooking like mine." Uncle Crusty (with a disdainful smile) : "Does he? Well, he's about right there, poor chap." "I WARN you,' said the old gipsy, solemnly, "that an enemy will cross your path." " Oh, ho !" laughed the scorcher, scornfully ; "if he's going to cross my path, you'd better warn him 1" NEIGHBOUR : "Good morning, Mr. Blank." Blank : " Good morning, sir." Neighbour: "How is Mrs. Blank this morning ?" Blank: "The doctor tells me she is at death's door, and I'm afraid he won't be able to pull her through." RIGHTEOUS INDIGNATION.—Mrs. Jones: "I won- der what it is that makes baby so wakeful ?" Mr. Jones (savagely): "Why, it's hereditary, of course I—this is what comes of your sitting up nights waiting for me !" THE DOUBTFUL POINT. —First Suburbanite (bit- terly) : "I'm blest if I think the average cook will ever get to heaven 1" Second Suburbanite: "Don't know; but it's very questionable whether she'll be willing to stay after she does get there." HE FELT SORRY.—Mrs. Hayhaw (in Kansas) : "They say that cyclone in the next county was the wust that ever happened in the State." Far- mer Ilayhaw : "That's too bad !—that's too bad 1 That 'un we had a few years ago was allus thought the wust on record; but them folks'll be able to crow over 'us after this." "As I came home in the shower," remarked Mr. Murray. Hill, "I saw Miss Homewood out with her rainy day costume on." "Oh, tell me all about it, replied Mrs. Murray Hill, eagerly. "I am deeply interested in rainy day costumes." "Well, I can't tell you very much, for I noticed uothing especially except her heliotrope stock- ings." SHORT-SIGHTED.—Ha: "It is Strange how fre- quently inventors fail to realise the importance of their own work." She : "What is the particular instance ?" He: "Why, here is a statement that the inventor of the hair-pin intended it to be used simply in dressing the hair 1" HEART.—With her own hands she had prepared his dinner. "Ha !" she muttered, aslis customary under these circumstances. At the Tast moment she concealed a poniard among the folds of her dress; for, although the way to a man's heart was through his stomach, it were best to anticipate possible failure. A SEVERE TEST OF FAlTH.—First Theosophist: "This settles it; I resign from the society." Second Theosophist: " What's the matter? " First Theosophist: "Why, one of my tenants has gone off without paying his rent, and left a note saying he would try to square up with me in some future existence !" _ _

NOT ENOUGH.—Kind Lady: "I am sure you would learn to love my children." Nurse: "What wages do you pay Kind Lady: "Four- teen shillings a month." Nurse: "I am afraid, ma'am, I could only be affectionate with them at that price." A PRISONER at the sessions had been duly con- victed of theft, when it was seen, on "proving previous convictions," that he had actually been in prison at the time the theft was committed. "Why didn't you say so?" asked the judge of the prisoner, angrily. "Your lordship, I was afraid of prejudicing the jury against me. A LITERARY ATROCITY.—WeyIer : "Did you hear of those cases in Cuba where the insurgents tortured peaceful citizens to death?" Old Ac- quaintance: "I read the accounts. It must have been an awful piece of work." Weyler : "Awful piece of work! Nothieg of the kind when a man is accustomed to writing in that style. Only took me a few minutes." LESSONS DISCONTINUED.—Friend: "What is the matter, Blankley ? You're all cut about and your arm in a sling, as though you had been in a fight, and yet you look beaming and smiling over it all." Iffankley "The fact is, I have all along thought my boy Harold a sort of muff, and I undertook to give him some boxing lessons. This is the result of the first lesson. Oh, I'm proud of that boy!" OF HONEST PARENTS.—" My opponent," shouted the orator, "has seen fit to refer to the fact that my mother took in washing. She did.; and, what is more to the point, she always-sent it all back I" After that there was nothing to do but cast a majority vote for the man whose parent showed such evidence of perfect honesty and attention to duty. WELCOME RELlEF.—Gentleman (just going, after having had his hair cut, to barber) : "I haven't met any barber like you for years." Barber: "Always try to do my best, air." Gentleman: "I'm referring to your originality. You are the only hairdresser during the last ten years .who hasn't told me my hair was getting thin on the top." WHAT TO DO WITH THE Boy.—A farmer in America had a son, and did not know what business to start him in. So he put him up in a room in which there was nothing but a Bible, an apple, and a dollar. He decided that if after a short time he found the boy eating the apple, he would make him a farmer; if reading the Bible, he would train him for the Church; and if he had rocketed the money, he would make him a stock- broker. Entering, he found the boy sitting on the Bible and eating the apple, with the dollar in his pocket. He became a "politician." "DEAR Sue," he whispered, "(10 you think if I married you your father would ever forgive us?" "I'm sure he would, dear," she asserted, softly. "And would he give us a house of our own?" "I know he woule, dearest." And would he give us enough to live beautifully on?" "I am sure of it, Harry." "And would he take me 'at° the firm?" "Certainly he would." "And let me run the business to suit myself ? " "Of course he would, darling." She snuggled to his bosom, but he put her aside, coldly. "I can never marry you, he said, hoarsely. "Your father is too willing to get you off his bands." MEISSONIER one day set a trap for his gardener by giving him some of the roe of a red herring and asking what seed it was. The gardener gave it a long name, and premised that it would bloom in about three weeks. Meissonier chuckled to him- self, and agreed to inspect the blooms in three weeks or more. When the time came the painter questioned his man about it, and in the hothouse, sure enough, were the blooms in the nature of the heads of six red herrings just emerging from the earth in the pot. Meissonier breathed a deep sigh, and shook his gardener's hand, exclaiming: "What a wonderful man you are ?" Hornims TASK.—" What strange methods some

men adopt to get wives !" she remarked as she looked up from the newspaper which she had quietly appropriated as her's by right because she was first at the breakfast-table. "What's hap- pened now?" he asked. "Why, a New York widower has made application for one at the Government Office where the immigrants land," she explained. "He says he wants a waman who is thoroughly respectable, of kindly dllposition, fairly good-looking, good to children, obedient"-- "Hold on t" he interrupted. "What's that Jut?" "Obedient." "He might as well give up." THE WORM TURNS. —The affable passenger had been searching for a victim for a long time. He had made exclamations when reading his paper, in the hope that it would attraet the attention of some one and give him the opportunity to show his power as a conversationalpt, but all his littie mess failed. The people who sat near him seemed to Da solely centred on themselves, but still he was not completely discouraged. He looked about him, and selecting one man whom he thought he might be able to impart much interesting information' he began operations by remarking: " rardon me, but you look very much like a man I know." The man who was addressed looked over the affable passen- ger gloomily, and, recognising the type, he replied, In tones that would cause the thermometer to sink, oven in the Klondike: "Yes, that is possibly so; fait at the same time you must excuse me, for yoi

div.head: WARRINGTON v. HALIFAX.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. HALIFAX.

This engagement on the Wildenpool enclosure was the Good Friday football fare provide, for local followers of the Rugby code and the match drew a crowd of at least 5,000. Not since the celebrated cup-tie match of two years ago when Warrington gave Halifax the " knock-out" blow, had we been favoured with the presence of the men from Halifax town on the Wilderspool ground. Their return visit aroused cdnsiderable interest and it was confidently anticipated that a good game would be witnessed. In this respect the spectators were not disappointed but the decision to play only 30 miuutes each way somewhat curtailed the enjoyment. The weather was eYceedingly fine and although the gale experi- enced early in the morning had somewhat abated,a high wind blew from goal to goal. Warrington did not place a strong team in the field. Both Isher- wood and Fish were given a rest and their places were taken by Lawless and Moores. Promptly to time, the teams turned out as follows : Warrington .—Hallam, back; Jones, Duckworth, Lawless, and Moores, three-quarters; Bate and Burgess, halt backs ; Taylor, Fairhurst, Swift, Scheltze, Board- man, Morrison, Eden and Jolley, forwards. Halifax :—Halliwell, back ; Mallison, Rigg, Nickol and Stoyte, threi quarters ; Jones and Litneton, half- backs ; Kitson, Langborn, Winskill, Bartle, Mitchell, Norton, Mallison. and Nutton, forwards. Having won the spin of the coin, the Warrington skipper elected to play with the wind behind him in the first half. Berle kicked off and the home team imme- diately went off with a rush and Burgess grassed Nickel under the goal posts. Lawless got peEsession from a scrimmage but failed to part with the ball and the advantage was lost. Bate picked up the ball from the feet of the visiting forwards and passed out to Moores who made progress along the touch until grared by two or three burly Halifax men. Warrington continthei the pressure and a penalty kick being awarded,Jones had a splendid opportunity to kick a goal i but failed,the ball travelling wide of the uprights. From the drop out,Taylor got possess7on and put in a fino punt. Lawless was cheered for a smart tackle. A comb!ned movement, initiated by Burgess and taken up by Duck- worth and Moores almost resulted in the latter scoring, he being pushed into touch abut a yard from the line. A penalty kick by Lawless was charged down but Hali- fax could make little headway and were kept busily defending their lines. Burgess tricked Littleton, bet was grassed before he could reach the line. ufing their feet well, Halifax reached the half way lien for the first time. Moores sent them back by a lefty punt which rolled over the dead ball line. War- rington continued the pressure and from a scrimmage Bare got nicely away and passed out to Schoitze who threw a good opening away by a pass forward. Bate came out brilliantly from the next scrimmage for, by a beautiful " sham " he tricked his oppenent and se-red a fine try. Jones tailed to kick a goal. From the restart Warrington again got into the visitors twenty- five and Lawless got nicely away but cropped the ball when a score seemed imminent. Passing between Littleten, Riee, Nickel and Stoyle gained ground,but the !act-named player was:erounded before becoming danger- ous. When the refere Vew his wrestle for half-zime, after thirty minutes play, Warrington were leading by tbree points to nil. Aided by the wind Halifax made an invasioe into W..rrineton teriitory but fine play by Bate and Burgess tracsferred play. I breakaway by the forwards in which Moirison and Sclioltze were to the fore almost ended In a score for ti:e home team, !ha keen tackling of Rine alone eyeing the Helef,x lines. IrViterington main- tained their foothold in the visiting twenty-five until the Halifax forwards made a desperate rush. It was now the visitors' turn t press but they rarely became dangerous. Bate and Burgess were a thorn in the aide of the visitors and made splendid openings for the hose-quarters. Jones was given an Opportunity but ie kicking over the line the ball rolled dead. Eialitex got down to the other end' and a mistake by Fairhurst let the visitors in. Tbe neetertunate mistake was made in this wise : Fairhtivit endeeveured to clear out the visitors by a punt, the ball went high into the air and the strong need flew it back over the W irrington line. Jones made an effort to drop on it but failed and La,nghorn rushing up, scored a try. !lige then kicked a fine goal aid placed the visitors two poiets ahead. A dieermined -fort wig mede by the Warringten men to increeee their Ecore, but having once gained the lead Halifax adopted purely defensive tactics and won the match by five points to three.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. BIRKENHEAD WANDERERS.

This Bank Holidr.y match was the concluding game of the season at Birkenhead. Warrington were without ,evcral leading players but the fifteen who crossed the Merrey proved quite eqoal to the task before them. Boisterous weather prevailed when Glover kicked off for the Wanderers against the sun and wind. Fish was prominent for Warrington at the start, and after run- ning well kicked a penalty goal. Aided by the gale, the visitors held the advantage, but the Wanderers played pluckily, and Edmunds and Glover were prominent. Off-side by Hellewell gave Warrington more ground. Ingham dashed away with smart dribbling, and Hallam chocked just in time. Tho game vras well contested. Davies, the Wanderers' half, was very selfish; otherwise his side would have been in a good position. Hard tackling did not suit on the hard turf, and players needed attention from the referee. A serum on theenome line looked bad for the Wanderers, but nothing happened, and Edmunds broke away to the centre. Just before the interval Fish kicked a second penalty goal, and at half-time the visitors lei by two voals to nil. Resuming, Clayton made a dashing run on the Birkenhead right wing. Lewis took a penalty kick, tut failed, as also did Hellewell shortly afterwards. At length Fish broke away and scored for Warrington, which put the visitors 7 points ahead. Warrington strove hard to improve their lead, but failed, and when the whistle blew they retired winners by two goals one try to nil.

div.head: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE CUP. First Round. Widnes y. Tvldesley.
div.p: SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE CUP. First Round. Widnes y. Tvldesley.

At Widnes on Tuesday neither team was at full strength, but the game was keenly contested. Widnes had a strong wind behind them, and attacked vigorously 13,:iwn scoring an unimproved try. A moment later he dropped at the goal,the ball hitting the upright. Then from a scrummage Rispan slipped over cleverly, and in rapid succession tries vr ere vered by Riley—after splen- did work by Lomas—and Peacock, who ran in twice, Kinsella placing a goal from the second. Tyldesley, notwithstanding that they were three men short, played up stubbornly, attacking towards the interval, but they were repulsed. Half-time arrived, with Widnes leading by seventeen points to nothing. Restarting, Widnes at- tacked, Halligan scoring after a smart run. Aspey failed at goal. Tyldesley, who had been strengthened by three late arrivals, now slaowed more vigour, and Alcrcd secured a smart try at the corner, but the goal kick was a failure. Midfield play followed. Aldred got possession at half-way, and scored for Widnes. Result:— Widnes, one goal and seven trite (twenty-three points) ; Tyldseley, two tries (six points).

div.head: RUNCORN v. WIGAN. Replayed Tie.
div.p: RUNCORN v. WIGAN. Replayed Tie.

The replayed tie between Runcorn and Wigan, in the West Lancashire and Border Towns Cup Competition, came og at the Irwell-lane enclosure, on Wednesday evening last. The kick-off was advertised for six o'clock, but at that time neither team had put in an appearance; and only a crowd of about 50, drowsed lazily about the rails, expectant, and wonder- ing what was likely to turn up next. Slight diversity eras caused by the arrival of the referee and linesmen ; then a few of the Runcorn men put in an appearaece and the crowd applauded. It was 625 however, before Wigan presented themselves and hostilities commenced. Runcorn had quite a representative team. Houghton was absent, but otherwise, some of the most able players who have figured throughout the season had donned the green. Wigan were also fairly represented. Farmer commenced, at which time the spectators had increased to about 300. Runcorn got the better of the opening exchanges, and for some time Wigan were kept in their own half. Butterworth and Jolley made the first efforts at scoring but were both held on the line. H. Farmer tried a penalty from a good position. and failed. Wigan then replied with spirit and Wilkinson was called up' n to save from Eidson. He did so, wi‘ h a beautiful sprint. The game then luctua.ted a bit either end being visited in turn. Assum- ing once mere a decided upper hand, Runcorn pressod, and as the result of passing between Richardson, J Butterworth, Warder and C Butterworth the latter got over. Farmer failed to convert. A peaalty followed and Farmer had his kick charged down. Richardson seemed in a lively mood, and touched down right under the pests. Farmer converted this time. J Butterworth ran in the next try. Farmer was again enable to improve from a difficult position.—Half-time : Runcorn, 1 goal, 3 tries (11 points) ; Wigan, nil.—Recommencing Runccrn bad matters their own way. Richardson secured the first try, which Farmer eon-

div.head: PROPOSED WIDNES AND RUNCORN TRANSPORTER BRIDGE.
div.p: THE PROPOSED WIDNES AND RUNCORN TRANSPORTER BRIDGE.

Mr. William Handley, chairman of the Parliamentary ante Gsneral Purposes Cemmittee of the Runcorn Urban District Council, in the C00i35 of an article on the above scheme contributed to a Liverpool contemporary, thus refers to etene of the principal clauses of the Bill now b ,fore Parliament :—" Daring its consideration by the House of Commons the Bill has been very mush enlargee. Orieinally it consisted of 33 clauees ; as amended in committee it now contains fifty-three, with numerous sub-sectional clauses. Of the new clauses six have been added at toe inscaoce of the Mersey Conamis- sieners, fully safeguaraing the navigation Of the river; core offered by the promoters,providing that the bridge shall not be used as a conveyer of brine pipes without the further coment of Parliament ; three, saving the rights of the Crown, the Duchy of Lancaster, and the owner- ship of reclaimed laud; one,providing for the subscribing and payment of capital. subject to the satisfacticn of the Board of Trade ; one, for she protection of the Man- chester Ship Canal Company ; cue, for the protection of , the Corporation of Widnes ; one, at the instance of the London and North-Western Railway COIN pany, for the discontinuance of the Runcorn Perry after the opening of the Transporter Bridge ; and one, making special pro- vieion for the use of eleetric power. There remains still to be added during its passage through the House of Lords a clause, with its sub-3ections, for the protection of the Urban District of Runcora, which, as submitted by the promoters, was accepted ter the Urban Council at its meeting held on the sth inst. The clause for the protection of the Corporation of Wid- nes contains ten sub-sections. By these the Bridge Com- pany engage to construct, light, and maintain suitable approaches to the shore of the river Mersey ; not to interfere with the present access to the ferry until an equally good one has bees substituted, nor to obstruct or interfere with the public right of way to the Victoria Promenade or Terrace-read;a,nd to construct the founda- tions and anchorage of the bridge,as approved by the Corporation. The company are to bear the cost of relay- ing any disturbed sewer, gas, or water main, and to pay for any damage occasioned by the execution of the works. These are to be subject to the reasonable approval and satisfaction of the Corp ration ; bat any case of dispute is to be subject to arbitration. The clause for the protection of the Manchester Ship Canal Company contains fourteen sectional sub- clauses, and is fraught with very great possi- bilities for the future development of the bridge, canal, and towns of Widnes and Runcorn. These Sub-sections state the span of the bridge is net to be less than I,OOOLt. from the mitres of the two main piers, anti also that the pier on the Cheshire side shall leave a clear width of 150 ft between it and the coaerete wall of the Ship Canal. This pier, it would seem, will have its foundations in the Ship Canal or on its , bank, but it is to be constructed at a depth eufficient to admit of the canal being deepened to a depth of 20f c ' In below ordnance datum. These conditions are inci- dent to the construction of a wharf to be made at this spot by the Ship Canal Company, at the expense of the Bridge Company, for which they are to provide a sum of £3,900 six months before the bridge is ready for open- ing, and a further sum of £2,000 for the enlargement of the wharf at the expiration of ten years from its open- ing,if so required by the increase of traffic. This wharf, though abutting on the canal, is to be for the joint use of both companies. Elaborate provision is made for smooth working as between the companies, both during and after the completion of the bridge and wharf and all other works incident thereto ; and any dispute or failure of agreement is to be settled by arbitration, under the direction of the Beard of Trade and the Arbitration Act, 1889. The clause to be added for the protection of the urban district of Runcorn contains six sub-sections, and penerally they are in agreement with the Widnes clautse, the differences being merely local, necessitated by the constraction of the intended wharf at the foot of Waterloo-road- The present access to the ferry is not te be removed until another satisfactory ene has been provided. The ferry will for a time be open as at present, but on the opening of the bridge for public traffic, the London and North-Western Railway Com- pany, as the owners of the ferry, will be enabled by a clause in the Act to absolutely cloee the ferry, and dis- continue its use. Sentiment may cause regret at this absolute closing of the "ancient ferry," of which there is historical evidence that for more than seven centuries it has existed as a highway between the Palatine Counties of Chester and Lancaster ; hut it will be readily admit- ted that the approaching twentieth ceratury imperatively demands methods .of ceaveyance more in accord with its needs than is or can be afforded by the provision of a small boat, propelled intermittently by scull or oar, as the state of the tide will allow, and that its supercession by a transporter bridge will b 3 an incalculable gain to the more than 50,000 inhabitents dwelling on the banks of the Mersey in the twin sister towns of Widnes and Runcorn."

div.p: THE EXAMINER, FIUDAV APRIL 20 1900
WARRINGTON CRICKET CLUB.
Next Season's Fixtures.

Appended will be found a list of the fixtures of both the first and second elevens of the Warrington Cricket Club. As will be seen: the day mstches are not so numerous on account of so many disastrous results attending them last season owing to the club being unable to put strong teams in the field. The new fixtures are with Bowdon, New Brighton and Whalley Range. The eleven will be somewhat similarly composed to that of last year. All last Season's players will _ . . . _

be available including the professional Thewlis. Hampson will occupy his usual place behind the wickets. It is very probable that Messrs. A and E Callon, brothers of Mr. J Callen of Widnes, will also throw in their lot with the Warrington Club this season. Mr J Callon has been a valuable playing memberof the club for sometime and his brothers have given every promise of making good cricketers by their performance in Widnes clubs last year. Of men in the second eleven who are likely to find a place in the first when necessity occurs are E Gibson who shows promise of being one of the best left-hand slow bowlers Warrington has produced, and J Thompson who promises to be a brilliant batsman, as was evidenced by his display against Leyland last year. Dr Smith will not undertake the captaincy this year on account of his profes- sional duties but whenever it is possible for him to play he will take the field. Mr J W Bibby will be the captain and last year he proved himself a very capable man for the post by the sound judgment he displayed in handling his men when he captained the team in the absence of Dr. Smith,

Major the Rev. E. P. Lowry, Sonic? Wesleyan Chaplain to the Forces, with the Rev. T. F. Falittler, Senior Church of England Chaplain, visited these trenches immediately after the Bocr. retreat from theil, mighty stronghold. Mr. Lowry writes to the 3 Methodist Recoraer ": " Of course I did not go to those trenches and laagers for purposes of loot. That is scarcely in my line, though naturally I picked up a few curios, as in duty bound. But the professional looters, who were there betimes, were in some cases well repaid for their 'trouble. We are told that in the tents of Boer officers diamond "rings and gold watches, and portmanteaus full of various valuables, were "found. The retreat must have been hurried enough to justify its being called a " rout ; and the line of retirement was for a /ono'b way littered wits abandoned spoils. "Large supplies of sundry kinds of food and clothing were left in the trenches "or beside them, and I was astonished to note how large a portion of the Boer "belongings had originally come from England. One of our poets tells us that
'Sympathy without relief Is like mustard without beef.'

"I saw no beef in the Boer trenches except in the, to us, repulsive form of stale " biltong. Of that there must have been tons left; but the mustard was there— "good old English, with the famous Bull's Head on the tin."
