div.head: tettcrs to Mt alttor.
div.p: tettcrs to Mt alttor.
A Curious Phenomenon on the War

Sir,—b your last ieaue " Ina" gave us six para- graphs headed" Sone Curious Phenomena of the War." With tbe main cmtention of five of the-e lam in full aceera ; men, esp.cielly with the penultimate o,e. I think with "Lena " that the State and not private charity should take up the respensinility of providing for those whose breadwinners have been called to the war. This should be a national duty. But it is in his third paragraph that" Iona" qualifies himsel for ad- mission ino the ranks of Curious Phenomena of the War. Curious indeed .is it to see peep!e—otherwise regarded as sane—persistently holding up the Boers as persecuted saints. now " fighting for liberty and independence.'d Well I grant you, it is liberty they are fighting for—but what sort of liberty? Was it that liberty which was alone worthy of the name—liberty all rouad—liberte to the full extent, consistent with good, citizenship ? But Kruger and Co., do not want this brand of liberty ; the liberty of license to enslave others is the article they reqnire, as the speaker at the Earlestown meeting repor- ted in your issue of the 7th.—Mr. J. fl. Profit seconded and said :—"Our best men were giving up their blood in the:struggle. We had beard a great deal about a certain raid, but he would like to ask tbe Boers if they had not heard of a certain raid also when Pretorius went in the country of a neighbouring chief and in addition to other acts of violence seized 17 childrer, and carried them off as slaves to tbeir own country. We had been a true brother to the Boer, we had assisted him when he was in bankruptcy, and when the Zulus might have eaten him up, we rescued him from their jaws. The Boers had floated our flag, they bad hindered and insulted our missionaries and had trodden down tha poor natives and had wronged our own country men. He hoped when peace came it would be permanent and prosnercus." And these are the oppressed people whose affi ctions make s "boa's" heart sore within him ! These the long suffering saints whose nnocence "lona." with that magnificent faith which overrides obvious facts be'ieves in ! Is it not indeed strange that "Iona" and his co-thinkers—or rather those like-minded with him—should be content to be Devils advanatee in such a cause ? Yours truly,
JOHN PEERS.
Ponketb, 16 April, 1900.

div.head: ST. HELENS,
div.p: ST. HELENS,
UNSATISFACTORY Ev ID EN CAI AT A ST. HELENS INQUEST.

Mr. Coroner Brighouse held an inquest at St. Helens Town Hall, on Tuesday. on the body of Patrick Blaney, aged 47, a labourer' of 18, Wright-street, who was killed at the works of the St. delens Copper Company,Limited Ravenlsead, belonging to Messrs. W J Thornson.hy being crushed between a waggon and the boiler-house. Mr. Kellett. Inspector of Workshops and Factories, was present on behalf of the Governuiert ; Mr. Oppenheim represented the company, and Mr. H L Riley,the widow. —The Coroner said deceased's work was to empty waggons of slack for the boilers. About a quarter-past five on Thursday last the yard foreman, James Saxon, and deceased were moving a couple of waggons containing slack, when deceased got on to the brake of one of the waggons, and was cruebed trtween it and the wall of the b)iler house. The rails and the boiler-beuse wall are oaly a very few inches apart. Saxon stated that be called out to Blaney to rand clear, but the poor tellow seemed to have run on to toe trake to stop the waggons going down the incline, wine the result that be was jammed between the wagenn and the wall.—Mrs. Blaney, widow of the uecease t, gave evidence of identification.— James Sexen, the yard fereman of the works, said that the waggons were goieg between the engine-house and tlw nsillhouse to the boiler-house. Be was in charge, adtl when going down aeceased jumped on to the brake. Witness was not aware of him getting on, and there was no necessity for him to take part in the operation of braking down. There was only about llin between the wall of the boiler-house and the ra)ls.—A long examin- ation of the witness by Mr. Riley and Mr. Oppenheim elicited contradictory statements.—Peter M•Donald said the waggons had travelled about 30t. when they Vera stopped on account of a gaspipe having fallen across the line. Witness gct on to the water tank and lifted the pipe up to allow the waggons to pass. Blaney got on to the brake of the first waggon, ;Lai they passed under where he was standing. He did not see the accident.—After further evidence, the Coroner said he must assume, and no doubt the j ary would do the same,that Blaney had taken Saxon's warn- ing for him to assist him (Saxon) in braking d mil the waggons, and had so got on the brake and been jammed between the wall and the waggon.—The jury returne I a verdict of" Accidental death," and raid that the evi- dence of all the witnesces was very unsatisfactory. They thought that it would have been better for them to have viewed the place w hete the accident happeeed.—The Coroner said that at Warrington and other Vacee a wag- gogette was provided for the jury to visit the works.

div.head: WAR.
div.p: THE WAR.
LATEST TELEGRAMS. General Carrington at
Beira.
Lorenzo Marquez, WEDNESDAY.

General Sir Frederick Carrington has arrived at Beira. The companies oE Australian Bushmen pre- cede him ny rail to Salisbury. It is expected that he will soon be within striking distance of blafe- king.
There is a report here that a Boer commando has been despatched to intercept General Carrington's force, but it is considered that it is unlikely to be of sufficient strength to cause any anxiety,
Roberts' Great Move. Expectation at Cape Town.
CAPE TOWN, WEDNESDAY, 6.55 P.M.

The war news here at present is stagnant, al- though everyone is on the tiptoe of expectation, pending the result of the movement which Lord Roberts is known to have started with a view to cutting off and surrounding the Boer commandos.
2,000 Cases of Sickness.
BLAMFONTRIN, TIIESDLT.

The heavy rains which have fallen during the last three days have greatly impeded the work of the transport branch. There are 2,000 ewes of sickness in the field hospitals. Most of them are due to dysentery and enteric fever. The :;ransport difficulties are delaying the equipment of the general /hospitals. Sixty patients left here to-day for the 6outh.

The Birkenhead detachment con4isted of four privates, ICcutsf )rd and district sent one subaltern, one corporal, and four privates. Another Runcorn Soldier finds a Billet in Pretoria.

Corporal George Attwood, of the South Lanca.hire Regiment, writing home to his mother, under date 12k March, says :—" We are at present at Pieter:n*li zburg, en route for the Cape. I understand the Cape Dutch are rising. We thought after the relief of Ladysmitn yr-3 would have had a rest, but it's Ike the policeman says, "move on." Bill Spencer (a Runcorn man who was missing after the Sp;on Bop engagement) is a priloner in Pretoria. lam very glad ; it might have t-e -n worse. How we came through that last engagement I don't know. We went straight to the Boer trenchesond drove them out with our bayonets. I regret to say tbat we lost our brave Colonel. He got shot whilst leading us, within 20 paces of the Boer trenches. Corporal Attwood forwarded with the letter the box which contained the Queen's gift of chocolate, put of which be sent home for his sister.

div.head: Departure of Captain George Cros-
div.p: Departure of Captain George Cros-
field and Lieutenant Broadbent from Southampton.

A Warrineton gentleman thus describes the departure of the es. Canada from Southampton on Saturday last: —Saturday was a beautiful sunny day at Southampton, and from early morning Imperial Yeomanry kept arriv- ing to embark on board the s. Canada. Fortunately tor the troopers there is a free refreshment stall pro• vided by the "Daily Mail." as the first meal on board is rather uncertain, -On board everything was very clean and comfortable, though the rank and file are packed together rather closely, haying to comerese theimelves into what is steerage in crdinary voyages. The saloesn accommodatien for ordinary times is given up to the officers and nurses, the latter on this oceasion numbering about twenty. It was quite two o'clock before the 77th Manchester Imoeriai Yeomanry, under Capt sin 0/oslHd, ateived. They had been travelling since 2.40 a.m., but looked very well. Part were berthed forward and part aft. Captain George Crosfield's state room was tastefudy decorated with flowers. - I'wo hours before the ship sailed the Duave,gan Castle, bringing Sir George White, Game up to the quay about 100 yard's off the Canada and not the least heerty welcome to him came from the 1,300 Imperial Yeomanry. At 3.30 the Canada was ready to follow the Gaul, which bad already left for the Cape. But as it was now low tide she lightly grounded, and it was nearly an hour before she Worked into the ch innel and finally got away. She was then a cnagnificnnt sight for the men had climbed into every available space, even up the rigging, and the declining sun shone on a wall of khaki relieved, here and there by red caps and red hocds of the nurses, by Union Jack and white wavisg hand- kerchiefs. Lieutenant Broadbent, of. Latchford was also on board. Miss Broadbent and Miss Gertrude Crosfield were present to wish their respective brothers adieu.

div.head: Shot and Shell a "Bit Comical." A Warrington Man at Ladysmith. • Siege Prices
div.p: Shot and Shell a "Bit Comical." A Warrington Man at Ladysmith. • Siege Prices

In a letter to , his mother, dated March 10-h, 1990, Private Picten, of the Ist Battalion Liverpool Reelment. says :—Thank God I have come out of the siege of Ladyttinith with a whole skin, end am able to send sou a few lines to tell you what we have heen doing since we left Wynberg. We rcaved instructions to proceed to Ladysmith last August, and the firs: engagement I went into was at Modder Spruit. Is was a bit comical, shots and shells flying over our heads ; anyhlw, we soon got used to it. It was more of an artilleiy duel, and so I ate my bread and cheese on the field. We retirrd aft,r elevon hours' fighting te Ladysmith. Our second affair was at Lombard's Kop, where we had the whole B -Cr I force out. Two days altr this our lines of communie4- tion were cut. We were besieged, and then ca-le the work of a Fiddler. up at all hours of the night building entrenchments, lsagers gun-pits, and wire entangle- ments in he front of the Boer cannonade. W. had plenty to eat for the first two months, and then the cap- On went down, an I you could not buy anylhing. This is a list Of some of the prices paid during thl siege : Eggs, 253 per dozen; lyeaci you could not buy; con- denied milk, 103 per tin ; tobacco could not be bou2hr, and cigarette, were 4s per packet. We had horse meat and brown bread, made out of meshes (that which , Kaffits eat).

div.p: THE EX ANJ IN I4T, FRI I Y, APRIL 20, 1900.
Corporal Chappell's Keepsake.

Corporal Chappell, of the 2nd Liverpool Regiment,who was wounded at the Orange River. on December 13, writing to his mother, Mrs. J. B. Chappell, of 7, Gres- venor-•errace, Wash-lane, says he has received the Queen's chocolate, which be will bring home when be returns, as be is afraid it would get loit through the post. fie says he is now able to sit up and move about in bed. He hopes to be on his way borne before long, and will writs from Netley. He does not think the war will list much longer, but the country will be in an un- settled state for a long time after it is over. The people here (Wynberg) are making great preparations for a procession, and they are also going to light a huge bon- fire on the top of Table Mountain when the relief of Malnking takes place, news of which is expected daily. He does not think ha will be able to get hold of any curios, as he will not be able to stop at Capetown, and the only curiosities up country are the Boers, but he has the bullet which was taken out of his thigh, which he has kept "for a k ensake." Lords Roberts and Kitchener, Sir Alfred Milner, Sir William MacCormac, and Hector Macdomald have 'visited him and others at No. 2 General

officer, a boon which is not often asked, and Tommy gets on very well *itnout it. Sometimms one of the officers will be rash enough to announce that be will stand the men a drink. When one realises what this means, one is forced to admit that the act indicates a generous and liberal puree. Such a drink implies no less than about 2,600 bottles of be r at twopence each or La 3.34 41, an unusual price, all will agree, for one drink."
RUNCORN NOTES.
my A CORRESPONDENT.]

T;ie confession of munier which was male to thp Runcorn Police last week has been sifted to the bottom, and as a result of the police inquiries the prisoner was on Thursday discharged. The story, however, is said to have been to some extent cor- roborated by two other men. Of one thing, how- ever, wo may now be certain, and that is that the man will trouble no more psrsons with his bogus confession as his eight days' detention has had a salutary effect upon him.

The 'election of Mr. W. H:Lndley to the position of Chairman of the Runcorn Urban District Council, is but conferring honour where honour is due. If there is one man who has done good service for the Runcorn public that man is Mr W Handley and that his services have at length been rewarded is a matter for congratulation. I cannot congratulate Mr Handley so much as I can congratulate the other members of tne Council, for Mr Handley has only received what he has earned many times over. But it is gratifying to . find that at length the Council have recognised and appreciated those qualities which so eminently fit the new Chairman for the post and duties he now enters upon.

If there is one thing more than another that I latest it is to smell the obnoxious odour tbat assaLs one's nostrils when certain tradespeople ace burning their rubbish heaps in their open yards. It was only so late as Thursday that a large establish- ment ran considerabls danger of being set on firs through this practice. Luckily the danger was averted, but why the public should be obliged to suffer the smoke and olfactory nuisance is beyond me. It should not be beyond the attention of the Urban Council, however.

The annual meeting of the Runcorn Rural Di,- tee-, Council will take place next Tuesday, and in the doe course of events the Council will elect its new chairman. The position for the last year has been admirably filled by Mr. Jot,eph Knowles, and I doubt whether the Ciuncil could do better than re-elect him.—The Board of Guardians, too, will elect their chairman. The retiring gentleman is Mr. J. Moseley Williams, and as he has filled tie post for the last few years, it, is quite on this books that he should retire, so as to allow of someone else sharing in the honour. Personally I should like to see the chairman of the House Committee (Mr. A. R. Norman) asked to accept the office for a term.

. I wonder whether Nit. Wisvvall had myself or my contemporaries in his mind when he referred " grumbling and pin pricks" at the meeting of the District Council, on Thursday last. If be had my- self,l would wish to point out that all my "grumb- ling and pin pricking" has been conscientious. Notwithstanding all that may be uriged to the con- trary, Runcorn is not the beau &cal that people would have us believe. There are many things re- quired; there are many things for which the rate- payers are paying that they have not got; and there have been grave faults committed by the Board of Commissioners and the Urban District Council in the past, which have turned out " bad for Runcorn." I will admit, however, that the Run- corn Urban District Council are now trying as they have for a fewyears Past to do their duty manfully, hut who can deny that the "grumbling and the pin pricking" does not keep thorn up to scratch?

Since 1 last wrote we hive had a v-ry hard t.me of •it, hog mercers under a hot sun and half and sometimes quarter rations aa yo l read in the papers. We marcnee a distance of 20 miles one diy under a burning sun, to move the B vrs out of their trenches, and although we were under fire, lam glad to siy we only had one man wounded and reaeaged te capture one of the enemy's guns for which we got great praise. div.head: Third South Lancashire Man's Adventures.
div.p: A Third South Lancashire Man's Adventures.

Writing to Mr. Hipkiss, 5, Hoyle-street, Warrington,C Maguire of the 3,c1 South Lancashire Militia; who pre- vious t• leaving for the Cape was employed in the roll turning department at Messrs Pearson and Knowles'. Bessey, stys We are at the time of writing 800 miles up in the country. The first place we wen:, to after we got off the boat wag Hanover. The Australians and Tasmanians were camped there. It was Saturday nieht when we arrivel, and on Sunday we were digging creeches: We were stopped as the scouts told us that -a party of 800-s were coining. There were only a few abets fired when the Boers retired. We took about a dozen of them prisoners. These we took to Naausvpoort At this place there is a hospital as well as a prise. We were in Hanover at the time the Rensburg fighting was going on, our battelion acting as rear guard. After the battle of Reesburg our battalion was divided into right and left halves. The right half battalion (to which I belong), went to Receberg, and the other half stopped at Arundel. Rena- burg was in a fine state when we got there. Horses were running about wild, Some being wounded: There were saddhs and all kinds of harnrss which belonged to the 13, am They put the:r dead in a hale and left them tine avered; we did the work for them. There were heavy' lessee on our aiee before the Boors retreated. I have been about 20 miles argued Renshurg an 1 from what three of us have seen the Boera have been cf.. ting rzady for years. Three of U 9 went out on horseback. We were so much intimated in going from one hill to another that when we turned to go back we found out that we were lost. You may guess what a sensation came over the three r,f us. As it was getting dark we da cot travel f o we had to let the horses go and we watt up The hills and stopped there till morning. Round about this place the B )ere had cemp.d at one time for there were scores of beasts o ly partly skinned. There were hundreds of sheet; skins and dead horses and the place fairly stunk. The n xt morning we could see a camp from the bill so we Lade for it. It turned cut to be the El iehlanders. They sent us hack with some of their szout4 and we got there about two o'cleck next morning. Thy had made sure we were taken prisoners. I got the stripe taken off and the other two got two hours drill every day for fourteen days. '[he officers admiral us in one way for having the pluck to go, bur said they would have to punish us, for if they let Us off other men would do the same especially whilst there were reenty of hrsesae knocking Menu". I found a shell near Ceesberg S-pje, al4 pounder. I brought it to csmp and gave it to the station maet,r. It is very hot in the day time, hut very cold at night. Dysentery is very' had amongst us. Two nut of our balslion did of it—but a !mod many of them briog it on themselvts by eating too much fruit."
Feeding "Tommy" on a Transport.

In the April number of the " Windsor Magazine" the e appears a particularly topical article on " Tommy's " life on board a Cape transport. Rega,rding his menu, we are told that "breakfast is at seven o'clnck, and rations of bread, lib a day, and either tea or coffee, are served out to the men. This is all Tommy is allowed for breakfast. Milk,augar, butt r and jim•are luxuties in which those only who can afford ttP(m may indulge. An idea of the extent of the extra supply will be gained from the fie that the men, numbering some 2.000, spent ov-r £BOO in luxuries during the voyage. This sounds a large sum in the aggregate, but it only avenges eight shillings a head for the seventeen days the voyage lasted, and therefore can searcely be called reckless extravagance on Tommy's part. The mana2ement of the commissariat department on a trans- port is no sinecure, and the task of handling successfully the enormous quarrities of stores needed on the vovags, and accurately dividing these into rations owl details, must be anything but nee. div.head: Cavalry Charge.
div.p: A Cavalry Charge.

Writing of " That Terrible Cavalry Charge," a eon- triblitor to the April part of " Cassell's Seturd ay Journal " says :—" 'f be popular conception of a cavalry cherge is teat a bedy of superbly meunted, brilliantly unif-rened soldiers hurl themsslves upon the enomv, sliashiug to right and left as they hew their way through his snake!' ranks. But the charge is by no means such A melodramatic occurrence as it is represented to be. In the first place, our cavalrymen do net take the field in the gay trappings which they wear at home. Efelinet arid plurnes--etven the cair ass of the bile Guards—are laid aside for the more serviceable khaki suit and pizh headgear. A cavalry charge is, hnwesser, a terrible sight enough without the theatrical touches that waving plumes and glittering hslmete would give to it. E kelt cavalry reeiment is divided int) four squadrons. Two squadrons constitute the right wing and two the left. When drawn up ready to charge the man are mustsree in two ranks, the rear rank being a hove's length be- hind the front rauk. About a horse's length or so in front of the regiment rides the e)mmending officer (a colonel) with, usually, a trumpeter on one hand and a subordinate officer on the eteer. The officers and non- commissioned officers are disposed at certain positions in their troops. When the °Mar to advance ia given the co onel orders his trumpet-r to sound the 'trot.' This cal is taken up by the trumpeters .t ached teach troop. 'Gallop shouts the colonel, and again the hu ?les ring out, whilst the horses, who know the calls as ',Mitts the m-n do, immediately obey the order. When close to tee enemy the colonel tie is the eagerly awaited Rome:tend to charge. A brief trumpet call conveys this to the regi- meet, who close in practe aliy knee to knte and force their horses torwsrd at trip speed. Con- trary to the 'general belief, the not-n do not cut w.th their swans, hut endeaveur to run through the enemy with these. To facilitate thrusting, c avalry swords are double-edged froin the point to atunt half -vay down. When going at full speed the impetus of the horse drise the sword thr sugh anyone whom it is pointed at But if cutting were attemptsd the stroke synti'd probtbly he too late, and the hors,ornln would stand a goad chance of eeliog pitehed out of his seat. Immedia`ely the regiment has f treed its way throitees the body of troops ir attacked the ' rally ' sounds, and wheeling round, the whole.mass charges back again. Mee forget danger when their blood is up,and soldiers who have seen much active service wiel t-11 you that to ride in a stile cavalry charge is the most exciting experience one can under- go."

div.head: 'DEATH OF CAPTAIN EDWARD
div.p: 'DEATH OF CAPTAIN EDWARD
DAVIES,

The inhabitants of Runcorn and Helsby will lie%r with proloui.d regret of the sudden death of Captain Ed ward Davie, which took place at his Runcorn residence, York-street, Runcorn, on Wedneaday evening last, after but 3 short though painful illness. On Thursday, Mr. Davies was about and amongst his friends as usual and hie hearty cheery disposition gave no indication that in a few short days he would be called away. On Good- Friday, he complained of being ill. Doctors were called in, and it was found the old gentleman, who w4B in his seventieth year, was suffering trom pleurisy, brenchitis,inflaenza and other complications. Very little tripe was entertained of his recovery after Monday, from which time he suffered greatly until he was happily released by death at six o'clock on Wednesday evening. Captain Davies WAS a very old and highly res- pected inhabitant of Runcorn, and during the Summer months rcsiderl at Helsby. He was well- known personally, and also by repute for his many unobstrusiva acts of charity. In the days before the canal, Captain Davies used to be the senior captain of the tugboats plying between Liverpool and Runcorn. When the Ship Canal Company undertaking was completed, however, Ciptain Davies was offered and accepted the post of superintendent and River' Surveyor to the Upper Mersey Navigation Commissioners a posltion he filled up to the very date of his death. In a.e discharge of his many and varied duties deceased was over painstaking and thorough. He was a true and ready friend and those in distress need not artily in vain: In politics Captain D•ViPS was very broad minded, and in religion he was ever a staunch Nonconformist. He held offize up to his death as a trustee of St. John's Presbyterian Chapel, of which place he was als) a faithful member. Captain Davie,.'s death will come as a severe blow to many as he was be- loved by those undor his charge, and respected by all to whom he was answerable. The, funeral is fixed for Saturday. .

The final score was—Warringsoe, thre,c goals three tries (15 points) ; Birkenhead, FLETCHER RUSSELL'S V. ALTRINCHAIII.—At Warrington on Saturday. The home team kicked off against a strong wind and sun. Altrincea.m mulled, and from the scrim- mage which followed Scott came very near scoring. Kicking by the visitors repeatedly sent the home team back until Scott, getting possession, scored after a good run, the kick at goal failing. Restarting, Altrincham pressed until Ceresas got away to centre, and Ashley scored for Altrincham. Half-time :—Altrincham 8 points Fletcher's, 6. The vieitore restarted, and pressed until a free kick relieved, and play went to the other end, where Scott dropped a goal. Fietcher's still kept up a vigorous attack,and Corless was almost over. Fletcher's bad an unsuccessful attempt to kick a goal, and play was rapidly taken to the other frit Result :—Fletcher Russell's 1 goal 2 tries (8 points) ; Altrincham, 1 goal 2 tries (8 points).
